history.title: Amazon: China-Linked Hackers’ AI Agents Exploited Medical Software Zero-Day
history.text: Amazon says autonomous AI agents run by a China-linked threat actor found and exploited a zero-day vulnerability in MONAI Label, an open source tool designed for AI-assisted annotation of medical images. The tech giant’s threat intelligence team detected the activity in September, after coming across an exposed instance of Cairn, an open source AI penetration testing framework. The instance had no authentication, so anyone could see the operator’s prompts and the agents’ output. The records showed a roughly 48-hour campaign against IP addresses belonging to universities in East Asia outside mainland China. The operator gave the agents a list of targets and told them to obtain shell access. After identifying the software on one target and mapping its API, the agents discovered a path traversal bug in a file upload function. “In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server,” Amazon said. In a later session, the agents used the flaw to plant a Python reverse shell in a file Python runs every time the interpreter starts, ultimately achieving a root shell. “Amazon Threat Intelligence assesses with high confidence that it was a zero-day based on the absence of any corresponding fix, issue, advisory, or prior mention in vulnerability databases for the affected open-source project,” the company said. The operator then gave the agents a proxy that tunneled into a second university and instructed them to target other devices on its network. “The server that the proxy connected to was running the same vulnerable software, and we infer the actor had used the zero-day to compromise it and establish the tunnel,” Amazon noted. The MONAI Label developers published an advisory this week. It rates the bug critical and says it affects versions 0.8.5 and earlier. Authentication is off by default, enabling anyone who can reach the server over the network to exploit the vulnerability. A fix has been created and will be included in the next release. Amazon has attributed the attack to an unidentified Chinese-nexus threat actor with moderate confidence, based on the language used in the prompts, the time zone in the scripts, and the fact that the targeted universities are likely of strategic interest to China. Related: European Commission Confirms AI-Assisted Cyberattack Disrupted Services Related: China-Linked Hackers Exploit PHP2Shell to Root Firewalls Related: Barracuda Hacked Amid Surge in Artex-Powered Cyberattacks
history.summary: Amazon's threat intelligence team discovered that China-linked actors used autonomous AI agents to exploit a zero-day path traversal vulnerability in MONAI Label, an open-source medical AI annotation tool. The agents mapped the application's API, arbitrarily wrote files to the server, and planted a Python reverse shell to achieve root access within about 11 minutes, targeting university networks in East Asia via an exposed, unauthenticated Cairn penetration testing framework. Amazon assesses with high confidence that the flaw was a zero-day, and the MONAI Label developers have since published a critical advisory affecting versions 0.8.5 and earlier, noting that authentication is off by default and a fix has been created for the next release.

history.title: A Single Malicious Webpage Let Researchers Hijack Meta Muse and Access Private Chats
history.text: A malicious webpage could extract a Meta Muse user's private conversations and stored memories from the assistant without triggering any approval prompt, researchers have shown. The same attack could be extended to reach the credentials Muse stores for the user's connected accounts. The work was a laboratory demonstration, not an attack on real users, and it stayed inside the individual user's cloud machine. NebuSec, the security firm that published it yesterday, says Muse's team has since fixed every weakness it describes. Muse is Meta's personal AI agent, launched on September 8, that works through the online accounts a user connects to it and can make purchases on their behalf. Each person's agent runs on its own cloud computer. There, a monitoring layer called Sentinel is meant to be the single gate for anything the agent sends out, and the passwords and tokens for connected accounts are supposed to stay beyond the agent's reach. Muse's team described the aim at launch: "So we designed the system to assume the agent may be under attack and limit the potential damage." In the demonstration, a malicious page the agent opened could pull a user's conversation history and stored memories to an external server and alter them, with no prompt shown to the user, according to the firm's research write-up. From there, the researchers chained a flaw in Muse's built-in browser, which the assistant uses for tasks such as creating PDFs, to a Linux kernel flaw, thereby taking full control of the user's cloud machine. They set out that chain in a technical breakdown. That full control reached the credential store, the saved files, and Sentinel itself, the parts Muse's security design keeps walled off from the agent. The compromise went no further than that one machine. The researchers did not break out to the shared server beneath it or into other users' machines. Muse was built to assume its own agent could be turned against the user and to box in any break-in. Each of those controls worked as designed, the firm said, yet the attack still ran the whole way through. The firm says it reported the findings to Muse's team and that the exploits were all fixed before publication. Meta has not publicly confirmed the fixes or commented on the work, and the write-up does not say whether any user data was accessed before the patches went in. The firm's Muse research broke into the cloud system behind the assistant, unlike an earlier Muse flaw found in September, which only let malware already on a user's Mac hijack the assistant on the device.
history.summary: A malicious webpage could extract Muse users' private conversations and stored memories without triggering any approval prompt, researchers showed. The attack chained a flaw in Muse's built-in browser with a Linux kernel flaw to gain full control of the user's cloud machine, reaching credentials, saved files, and the Sentinel monitoring layer. NebuSec reported the findings, and Muse's team fixed all described weaknesses before publication, though Meta has not publicly confirmed the fixes.

history.title: GnuPG Warns Critical GPGME Flaw Could Expose App Data via Malicious OpenPGP Keys
history.text: A malicious OpenPGP key with an unusually long user ID can trigger a critical memory bug in GPGME, the standard library that programs use to work with GnuPG. The GnuPG project warned yesterday that the flaw could be used to steal data from affected applications and has released fixed versions. The bug, tracked as CVE-2026-129975, affects all software that uses GPGME before version 2.3.0, whether the library is loaded as a shared library, a Windows DLL, or statically linked into the program. Examples the project gives include most mail clients, many XMPP clients, Samba, and its own Gpg4win, GnuPG Desktop, and GnuPG VS-Desktop packages. The project has not reported any attacks exploiting the flaw, and it notes that remote code execution cannot be ruled out. Its example of a path to the bug is signed data sent to an application. Which programs pass such material to the library without a manual key import is not something the advisory says. The flaw is a double free, meaning the same memory is released twice. It sits in two routines, read_status() and read_colon_line(), that read status lines and key listings coming back from GnuPG. When the input runs long, the routines move the data to a larger buffer but record the new address only if they finish without errors. An error in between leaves a pointer to memory that was already freed, and cleanup then frees it a second time, as the project's tracker entry details. The flaw was found by Johan Carlsson and reported to the project by GitLab last week. Disclosure was set for November 25, the advisory says, and moved up because the new Ruby2Shell bug forced the company to update earlier. What to Update The fixed library version is GPGME 2.3.1, released this week. A version 2.3.0 was never publicly available. What to install depends on where the library sits: - Shared library or DLL: update to GPGME 2.3.1, available from the project's official downloads and detailed in its security advisory. - Windows: Gpg4win 5.1.2 bundles the fixed library. Its release notes call the issue severe and say to update as soon as possible. - Older versions that cannot move to 2.3.1: the advisory carries a patch, and the legacy branch has its own fixed release, 1.24.4, whose legacy release notes say the project cannot guarantee that the branch will see every security patch. - Bundled and statically linked copies: these are affected too, and updates to the system's shared library do not reach them, so the applications that contain them need their own rebuilt releases. - GPGMEPP and GPGMEQT: no update is needed. The advisory offers no interim workaround for software that cannot update yet.
history.summary: GnuPG warned of a critical double-free flaw in GPGME (CVE-2026-129975) triggered by malicious OpenPGP keys with unusually long user IDs, which could expose application data. The bug affects all software using GPGME before version 2.3.0 and resides in `read_status()` and `read_colon_line()`, where input errors leave pointers to already-freed memory, causing a second free. The GnuPG project released fixed versions and related updates to resolve the issue.

history.title: Signal Blocks AI Agents From Reading Private Chats via Screenshots on Android and iOS
history.text: Signal has announced that it will restrict screenshots by default to stop artificial intelligence (AI) agents from reading private chats on Android and iOS devices, but conceded that the protection is "incomplete." The feature applies to agentic systems built into iOS 27 and on Android versions where the encrypted messaging platform can detect an AI assistant attempting to read the Signal screen. It also builds upon a similar setting that Signal introduced in Windows 11 last May following Microsoft's release of the controversial Recall feature. Calling the agentic integrations into Android, iOS, and Windows an "existential threat to Signal," Meredith Whittaker, president of the Signal Foundation, said the move is designed to uphold its privacy guarantees in the AI era. "In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents 'scan' the information that's on your screen," Whittaker said. "In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding." "The net result is that these AI capabilities in the operating system are undermining Signal's ability to independently guarantee privacy." The risk here is that AI agents can capture and store the information accessed from Signal either locally or on remote servers, with the activity occurring outside of the platform's control and potentially putting the privacy of all the participants in a conversation at risk. Users who want to disable the option can do so by navigating to Settings > Privacy > App Security > toggle "Block Siri AI" (on iOS) or "Screen security" (on Android). "However, doing so will potentially expose your (and your contacts') Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees," Signal said. "Our remedy is also incomplete – while we are doing everything we can, restricting screenshots does not address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data, such as retrieving content already present on a user's device via the file system." Signal also pointed out that application developers lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from eroding application-level privacy. It also called out the companies for failing to provide adequate documentation about how these systems work to help design necessary controls to prevent the agents from accessing sensitive application data. Specifically, it's urging the tech giants to provide "two common-sense remedies" to help protect the privacy of its users - - Access to easy and well-documented way to opt their app out of AI data access and processing entirely, including screen reading, filesystem access, notifications, APIs, and other OS frameworks, without making drastic compromises to the core user experience - Create better documentation and technical specifications around how AI agents function, specifically with regards to data access and processing The concerns are not theoretical. Reuters recently reported that Muse, Meta's AI agent, was able to bypass its own official "Connector" tool to obtain access to Signal messages on both an Apple computer and an Android device by taking advantage of the broad operating system permissions granted to it during initial setup. On macOS, for example, the agent leveraged macOS's accessibility and screenshot tools to navigate to the Signal app, take screenshots, extract text from those images, and regenerate the textual content within the Muse app. On Android, it read messages by abusing its access to the device's push notifications. In one case highlighted by the news agency, the AI agent alerted a Meta staffer using Muse on her personal phone with a reminder to respond to a message from her sister on Signal. "This seems like an extreme privacy violation. I definitely did not grant it access to other apps, or recall being asked about this," the employee said in an internal post. "We also see a growing need for tools that can prevent third-party agents, like Meta's Muse, from accessing application data using the deep permissions that users are encouraged to grant them during setup," Whittaker said. "In many cases these agents are leveraging accessibility settings that were meant to empower actual people to get the most out of their apps and services, not to act as a skeleton key that provides access to AI agents." Late last month, Apple released iOS 27.2 with an "Excluded Apps" option that lets users choose which apps Siri, Search, and suggestions can access. With Google Gemini, users have the ability to disconnect apps via the Connected Apps settings. Earlier this week, the iPhone maker also previewed new controls that allow Mac users to give more granular access to data they give to apps, including those that use artificial intelligence (AI) agents.

history.title: Cleverbridge warns hackers stole credit card numbers, CVVs in data breach
history.text: E-commerce platform Cleverbridge is warning that hackers breached its systems and stole customers' payment card information, including credit card numbers and CVV security codes. Cleverbridge provides e-commerce services to software and SaaS companies, allowing them to sell products, process payments, and manage subscriptions. The company lists numerous technology brands as its customers, including Red Hat, SUSE, Tenable, Veeam, Jamf, Sony, and Parallels. However, it has not disclosed which businesses' customers were impacted by the breach. In a new page about the security incident, Cleverbridge says it detected unauthorized activity on November 4, 2026, and temporarily took systems offline to contain the breach. "All systems were brought back online on 4 November 2026; however, our investigation subsequently determined that a third party copied payment card data stored on our platform," reads the security incident disclosure. Cleverbridge began notifying affected customers on November 20, warning that hackers had stolen payment card details used to make purchases through its platform. While its public disclosure confirms the theft of payment card data, it does not specify which card details were stolen, instead referring affected customers to their individual notifications for more information. However, a breach notification shared with BleepingComputer reveals that the stolen information includes payment card numbers, expiration dates, and CVV/CVC security codes. "Based on our investigation to date, the information involved includes the payment card details you used to make a purchase through Cleverbridge, notably your card number, expiry date, card security code (CVV/CVC)," reads the notification. "Note however that no other personal data (for example your name, contact or billing details) were copied. The affected card ends in XXXX." BleepingComputer redacted the last four digits of the affected payment card. The company has not disclosed how the attackers gained access to its platform, how long they remained in its systems, or how many customers were affected by the breach. Of particular concern is the theft of CVV/CVC security codes, which are used to verify payment card transactions. Cleverbridge also confirmed that the incident was not a ransomware attack and that attackers did not encrypt any of its systems. The company says it has notified data protection authorities, law enforcement, payment card networks, and payment partners about the incident. Cleverbridge is also working with TransUnion's Cyberscout to distribute breach notifications and provide affected customers with complimentary credit monitoring and fraud assistance. Affected customers are told to review their payment card statements for unauthorized transactions. Cleverbridge also recommends contacting card issuers about the incident, as banks may decide to replace compromised cards. BleepingComputer contacted Cleverbridge with questions about how many customers were affected, how the attackers accessed its systems, whether the stolen payment card data was encrypted, and why CVV/CVC security codes were accessible. history.title: OpenRouter Drops 3 Providers After Researchers Catch Months of Prompt Theft at AI Hosting Firms
history.text: Attackers stole data from inside three AI inference providers for months, and none of the three knew until researchers told them, the industrial cybersecurity company Dragos said this week. Some of the stolen requests were flagged as Zero Data Retention, the setting that is supposed to mean a prompt is never stored. OpenRouter, a gateway that routes customers' AI requests to a pool of third-party providers, said today that it has removed three providers from its platform, removed 125 endpoints from eligibility for Zero Data Retention, and notified all potentially affected customers. The findings showed no breach of OpenRouter itself, the company said. The earliest of the three breaches began in mid-July. The planted prompts were bait, but they were processed alongside real customer requests, and those were almost certainly copied too, the firm said. The finding comes from canary token research that seeded about two million prompts with unique web links and credentials between July and November, then watched for anyone using them. A planted secret can only be learned in one place, so any use of it means someone read the prompt that carried it. The largest of the three breaches involved a couple hundred AWS keys that were planted, each sent in exactly one request to one provider during a few short windows in late October. Every request sent during those windows was stolen, and some came from requests the provider had rejected before a model ever ran, indicating the attacker was copying traffic at the first point of arrival rather than deeper in the inference stack. The thief tested keys within hours in some cases, listed S3 buckets, searched Secrets Manager and Parameter Store, and tried to create Bedrock API keys and add IAM users to keep access, driving tens of thousands of AWS API calls. One attacker appears to have compromised two of the providers at once, using secrets from both from a single rented server. On November 1, the same attacker brought in ARTEX, an AI-driven penetration testing framework, and used it only to confirm that keys it already held were still live. Two of its user agents, artex-agent and artex-judge-r121, appear in no public indicator list the firm could find and are worth adding to detections. "A privacy flag doesn't help when the attacker is already inside," wrote HD Moore, the firm's chief research officer. The second finding needed no break-in. Sellers on an AI inference marketplace listed models at the lowest prices, enabled request logging, and collected what flowed through, the research found. The people doing it looked like individuals on home internet connections. One, working from a Mac on home broadband in France, took passwords from two prompts and typed root SSH login attempts by hand, then used the same machine to test several planted AWS keys. One of those keys had traveled through a different router that quietly forwarded some of its traffic to the marketplace, a hop that no customer was told about. That router has since told the firm it stopped, and route tracing across about 2,000 paths found several hundred unidentified systems, plus one seller that quietly adds about 1,000 hidden tokens to every prompt. A Chinese AI lab, which the research does not name, fetched the secret links from more than half of the seeded prompts sent to its models between July and October, including about two-thirds of the requests marked no data collection or Zero Data Retention. Prompts sent to U.S. hosting providers that resell the lab's models triggered the same scraper, thereby flowing back to the lab. A git client on another cloud later tried to clone private repositories referenced in the prompts, but only for that lab's models, and one large U.S. provider kept crawling a secret link more than two months after a single request to its search endpoint. Twenty-four days after one prompt was sent, its secret link was posted into a chat on Feishu, the Chinese workplace app known as Lark elsewhere. The link was opened within two minutes from three desktops and three phones in Beijing and Shanghai. The firm had disclosed only the first 8 characters of the provider's link, so whoever posted it was reading a cached copy of the full prompt. In practice, Moore wrote, the flagged prompts were kept, passed to other companies, and read by human beings. OpenRouter said in an incident announcement that the 125 endpoints removed from Zero Data Retention eligibility cover providers flagged by the researchers plus others cut as a precaution. Any endpoint removed during the review will require assurances and validation before its status is returned. The gateway is adapting the researchers' testing approach so that the checks can run on an ongoing basis and is verifying network paths to identify where requests and responses may be forwarded to third parties. The researchers are now working with about a dozen providers, and planted keys and secret links were still being accessed months after the first thefts, as of this week. Railway, a platform company, said in October that an intrusion it suffered was likely part of a series of attacks built to target platform companies with the end goal of compromising AI inference providers. Not all affected providers have posted publicly, the gateway said, and it has notified affected users either way. Three have posted. What the Providers Have Disclosed An attacker took control of an inference server at Phala and could view request data while it was being processed, the provider said in a preliminary incident report last week. The incident was contained on November 8, and the model service has been restored with added protections. Requests to the DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 model that reached Phala through the gateway between October 21 at 00:00 UTC and November 8 at 05:35 UTC should be treated as exposed, the report says, and every key, token, password, or other secret within them should be rotated. A third-party researcher had been placing unique canary credentials in requests since July 1, and only the ones sent on October 21 and 22 were later misused. Those tests sampled traffic rather than monitoring every request, so the provider maintains the broader precautionary window. At Together AI, an unauthorized party downloaded stored samples of customer prompts after an AI coding agent committed a credential to the company's public GitHub repository, the company said yesterday in a security notice. The samples had been collected for routine software testing and were generated by requests to the MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2, and Kimi K2.6 models in June and July. The party searched the samples for credentials to other services and tested them, and five of the tested credentials were canaries from the researchers' experiment. The company said it has no reason to believe the data went further, understands it has been deleted, and has made zero data retention the default for new accounts. Novita, another provider on the gateway, confirmed this week in a privacy notice that a routing configuration issue caused some MiniMax requests to be sent on to MiniMax's official API, beyond what was intended for those customers. Dragos has not named the three breached providers, OpenRouter has not named the three it removed, and neither has said publicly whether they are the same three. The provider behind the mid-July breach first blamed an internal misconfiguration, then a partner's data processing, before its own investigation found that attackers had compromised its internal credentials, the researchers said. It had still not disclosed the incident publicly as of this week. What Users Should Do The researchers' advice starts from one limit: a privacy flag binds only the first hop, Moore wrote, and AI agents will send whatever they can read, credentials included. Where a prompt goes is a choice, he wrote, and a customer who does not choose hands the choice to the lowest price. Self-hosting is the only option in which no third party reads a prompt, and going directly to a first-tier provider leaves one company, one contract, and one privacy policy to check. Routers need more care: pick the upstream providers yourself instead of accepting the default pool, verify that privacy settings actually change where requests go, and stay away from reseller marketplaces, some of whose capacity runs on stolen keys. A fake credential seeded into the context that agents and pipelines already send serves as a tripwire if any use of it is treated as an incident, and a free Thinkst Canarytoken is enough to get started. Settings that scrub known credential formats from prompts help too, though they miss sensitive data that is not shaped like a key.
history.summary: OpenRouter removed three providers and 125 endpoints from Zero Data Retention eligibility after researchers found attackers stole data from AI inference providers for months by embedding canary tokens in prompts, with the earliest breach starting in mid-July and the largest involving hundreds of AWS keys extracted from traffic at the first point of arrival. A separate issue involved marketplace sellers and resellers quietly logging and forwarding prompts, including one that added hidden tokens to every request and another that routed traffic through unidentified systems, while a Chinese AI lab accessed secret links from over half of Zero Data Retention prompts, causing them to flow back to U.S. resellers.

history.title: FBI Investigating Apparent Hack of Its Key National Criminal Justice Database, AP Source Says
history.text: The FBI is investigating an apparent hack of a national law enforcement database that it maintains, a person familiar with the matter said Saturday. The National Crime Information Center, known as the NCIC, is a computerized database of criminal justice information that is available to local, state and federal law enforcement agencies and includes records on fugitives, missing persons, criminal history data, stolen property and other topics. The FBI declined to comment Saturday on the apparent hack, which was first reported by CNN and confirmed to The Associated Press by a person familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak by name and spoke on the condition of anonymity. The scope of the problem was not immediately clear. Asked about the subject on Saturday, President Donald Trump said in a Fox News Channel interview: “We just heard about it, and I will say that it’s not good.” News that the NCIC was targeted comes as the country has encountered a series of digital outages in the government and private sector that Trump administration officials have said were caused by routine efforts to upgrade computer systems and fix vulnerabilities, rather than a cyberattack. There was no immediate indication that the FBI incident was related to those outages. The bureau has historically been a frequent target for hackers. In September, for instance, a criminal hacking group known as ShinyHunters revealed that it had obtained a massive trove of data on FBI employees and applicants and had compromised the bureau’s jobs portal. And in March, the FBI disclosed that it was investigating “suspicious activities” on an internal system that contains sensitive information related to surveillance operations and investigations. Related: Ransomware Response Expert Arrested in ShinyHunters FBI Hack Probe Related: ShinyHunters Claims FBI Hack, Demands Retraction of Threat Report
history.summary: FBI is investigating an apparent hack of the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database. The NCIC is a computerized database of criminal justice information accessible to law enforcement, containing records on fugitives, missing persons, criminal history, and stolen property. The scope of the problem is not yet clear, and President Trump commented that it "is not good," while administration officials have attributed other recent digital outages to routine system upgrades rather than cyberattacks, with no immediate indication the NCIC incident is related.

history.title: Rackspace Spot breach let hackers access customer Kubernetes secrets
history.text: Rackspace warned customers that hackers breached its Rackspace Spot cloud platform using compromised credentials, allowing them to deploy unauthorized workloads and access Kubernetes secrets in customer clusters. Rackspace Spot is a cloud platform that allows organizations to deploy and manage containerized applications using Kubernetes. The company disclosed the breach in a notification sent to affected customers and obtained by BleepingComputer, stating that attackers accessed parts of the platform on November 17, 2026, between approximately 00:20 and 22:00 UTC. Rackspace says it learned of the intrusion on November 18 after receiving a customer report and confirmed that the recipient's organization was affected that same day. "On 17 November 2026 (about 00:20–22:00 UTC), an unauthorized party used leaked credentials to access parts of Rackspace Spot," reads the notification. According to Rackspace, the attackers were able to act as legitimate users in some customer organizations, allowing them to create pods in Kubernetes clusters, read Kubernetes Secrets, and list nodes and volumes. Kubernetes Secrets store sensitive information such as passwords, authentication tokens, and API keys that can be used to access databases, cloud services, and other systems. Rackspace warned that the attackers could have read any Secret stored in an affected user's clusters, as well as any Spot API tokens or refresh tokens held by that user. The company says it has since revoked affected tokens and sessions, removed the unauthorized pods, rotated keys, and strengthened access controls and monitoring. Affected customers have been instructed to reissue their Spot API tokens, replace refresh tokens used in automation tools, download fresh Kubernetes configuration files, and rotate credentials stored in their cluster Secrets. Rackspace also advised customers to analyze logs associated with databases, container registries, Git repositories, cloud storage, and third-party services dating back to November 17 to identify possible abuse of exposed credentials. The company shared the following indicators of compromise associated with the attack: - IP address: 23.224.79.106 - IP range: 23.224.0.0/15 - Suspicious Kubernetes pod and object prefixes: i1, glm-, and probe BleepingComputer contacted Rackspace to ask how many customers were affected and whether customer data was stolen, but has not received a response. The breach also caused an extended outage of the Rackspace Spot administration console, temporarily preventing customers from managing their clusters and rotating potentially compromised credentials. In a Reddit discussion, Sirish Raghuram, co-founder and Chief Growth Officer of Platform9, which co-developed Rackspace Spot with Rackspace, explained that the company deliberately disabled access while securing its infrastructure. "I've been instrumental in creating Spot and in its operations to date, and I can tell you that the team and I are incredibly disappointed to have let you down in this way," Raghuram said. "I know you disagree, but we made the decision that shutting all access down and sanitizing the entire environment is what we can do to best protect everyone using Spot." After multiple delays, Rackspace announced that service had been fully restored on November 21. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. Attackers acted as legitimate users, creating pods, reading Kubernetes Secrets containing passwords and tokens, and listing nodes and volumes, with Rackspace confirming the intrusion the next day after a customer report.

history.title: Researchers Demonstrate Ghostscript Sandbox-Escape RCE via Crafted File Uploads in Popular Apps
history.text: A now-patched flaw in Ghostscript allows a crafted file to escape the program's security sandbox and run commands on the server that processes it. Ghostscript is the interpreter that many Linux servers use to convert uploaded PDFs, PostScript files, and images into other formats, often without the application calling it directly. Security firm pwn.ai showed this week that ordinary upload, preview, and print features in about ten common applications could be tricked into feeding it such a file. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-125396, was fixed on September 8, and there have been no reports of it being used in attacks. Getting a crafted file to Ghostscript is easy, because an application does not have to call it directly. A common image or document library such as ImageMagick, Pillow, libvips, or a Qt plugin will hand PostScript or EPS content to Ghostscript to render, even when the file is named .png, .jpg, or .pdf. A routine feature like making a thumbnail or cropping a picture can start the interpreter, and the exact path depends on the libraries the application uses. The underlying bug is a use-after-free in the part of Ghostscript that loads fonts. A crafted document uses it to switch off the checks in -dSAFER, the sandbox that is supposed to stop the document from running commands or reaching files. The security firm demonstrated the result by feeding such a document through about ten applications and watching a command run on the server, each time as the low-privilege account that does the rendering. Several of those paths needed no login: an anonymous print job to a shared Debian 13 queue, an emailed attachment that Roundcube webmail processed the moment the recipient opened the message, and public upload forms in the WordPress plugins Forminator and Essential Addons for Elementor. WordPress Core itself needed more: an account with the ability to upload files, which Authors and higher roles have by default. Although the CVE is classified as a local flaw, the firm's tests reached Ghostscript from the network via print jobs, email, and web uploads. The tested version and the access needed for each application are set out in its impact index. Artifex, which develops Ghostscript, fixed the flaw in version 10.08.0 on September 8, and is moving the vulnerable internal step into safer code. Ken Sharp, the developer who handled the fix, called that step "an ancient piece of code well known to be a vulnerability, but difficult to eradicate" in the bug report. The CVE was published last week and is scored 8.5 out of 10 in its security advisory. WordPress had already closed its own upload path in version 7.0.4 on August 12, under a separate identifier, CVE-2026-65640, as noted in its release notes. That fix and the Ghostscript fix cover different points in the same chain, so updating one does not remove the need for the other. Updating the Renderer The fix helps only where it reaches the renderer the application actually uses. Updating the host operating system does not update a separate copy of Ghostscript bundled inside a container image or an application, so a document worker can keep running the old code after the host package is replaced. Coverage across Linux distributions is uneven. As of last week, several still shipped a vulnerable Ghostscript or had a fix pending, according to the firm's survey. The list records package status, not a tested attack path for each system: - Debian 12 (Bookworm): listed as vulnerable - Amazon Linux 2, 2023, and 2027 Preview: fix pending - SUSE Linux Enterprise 12 SP5 and parts of 15: fix in progress - SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 16.0 and 16.1: fix in progress - openSUSE Leap 16.0 and 16.1: affected The firm did not establish whether current Red Hat, Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux, Oracle Linux, or stable Fedora packages carry the fix. Until the renderer is updated, the exposure can be reduced by requiring authentication on print queues and by limiting which file types an image processor accepts. System controls help too, and in one test an AppArmor profile stopped the compromised interpreter from starting a shell. One published proof-of-concept file, described in its technical analysis, shows only the core memory trick. It changes a value inside the running interpreter and sets it back, without running a shell command or touching files on the host, and on the patched 10.08.0 build it fails before that point. The firm's broader research extended to production services, including Google, which fixed the affected path last week. Its reports of similar problems at Dropbox and other unnamed services are separate Ghostscript bugs, not this one.
history.summary: A patched flaw in Ghostscript (CVE-2026-125396) allows a crafted file to escape its security sandbox and run commands on the server, affecting many applications that process PDFs, PostScript, or images without directly calling Ghostscript. Security firm pwn.ai demonstrated the exploit through about ten common apps, including print jobs, email attachments, and WordPress plugins, reaching the interpreter as a low-privilege rendering account, with the bug being a use-after-free in font loading that disables -dSAFER checks. Fix: The flaw was fixed in Ghostscript 10.08.0 on September 8, and WordPress already closed its related upload path in version 7.0.4 under CVE-2026-65640, though both fixes are needed as they cover different points in the same chain.

history.title: Hackers exploit GL.iNet cloud flaw to infect routers, KVM devices
history.text: GL.iNet has confirmed that hackers exploited a vulnerability in its cloud remote management services to install custom malware on customers' routers and KVM devices, with some affected users reporting backdoors and reverse shells giving remote access to infected devices. GL.iNet manufactures networking equipment, including home and travel routers, as well as KVM devices that allow users to access and control computers remotely. Its GoodCloud platform allows customers to remotely manage supported devices, including accessing and controlling computers and servers connected to its KVM products. In a security advisory published on November 20, GL.iNet confirmed that an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in its cloud remote management services to access devices and install malicious software. "The attack path has been blocked. We fixed the cloud vulnerability and blocked the access used in this incident," the company said. "Devices can no longer be newly infected through this attack path. These measures do not remove malware from devices that were already infected." GL.iNet has not disclosed how the attackers exploited its cloud platform, how many customers were impacted, or whether information was stolen from compromised devices. The company is also investigating whether computers connected to infected KVM devices were compromised. GL.iNet recommends that customers check their devices for signs of infection and install the latest security firmware, even if no malware is detected. The company's initial instructions told customers to look for a process running as crond -i /tmp/.log, which GL.iNet said was an indicator of compromise. While the cloud vulnerability has been fixed, GL.iNet says stable firmware updates containing additional security fixes for both routers and KVM devices are scheduled for release on November 22, 2026. For KVM devices, customers can follow the company's firmware upgrade guidance, which recommends version 1.10.3 or later for the RM10, RM1, RM1V2, RM1PE, and RM4PE, version 1.10.3 beta or later for the RM10RC, and version 1.8.7 or later for the RMQ1. Router owners should install the latest security firmware for their specific model as soon as it becomes available. However, GL.iNet forum members warn that the company's detection instructions may not identify all compromised devices, including those infected with other backdoors or running reverse shells. GL.iNet has linked to a community-developed detection and cleanup tool as part of the company's official support instructions for routers and KVM devices. The scanner performs additional checks for known malware files, suspicious processes, modified system utilities, and configuration files modified for persistence. It can also collect forensic evidence and optionally remove known malware components. The project's developers warn that the scanner cannot detect every infection and that compromised devices may require reinstalling firmware without retaining existing settings, as malicious files stored in configuration directories could survive an ordinary firmware upgrade. Customers who suspect their devices were compromised should preserve evidence before resetting them, avoid restoring potentially infected configurations, and rotate credentials and access keys that may have been exposed. GL.iNet also asked customers who run the scanner to upload the anonymous report when prompted so the developers can determine the number and types of devices impacted. For KVM users, the malware may have allowed access to the computers controlled by the KVM, so those devices should also be analyzed for potential compromise. Malware and reverse shells discovered Following the disclosure, GL.iNet customers and security researchers shared evidence of custom malware infections designed specifically for GL.iNET devices, as well as root-level reverse shells that connected compromised routers to the IP address 170.39.226[.]219. The reverse shells used the Linux nc utility to create outbound connections, allowing remote attackers to execute commands on infected devices. Researchers at RemoteToHome Consulting also identified a potential command injection vulnerability in GL.iNet's GoodCloud client involving a handler used for AstroWarp/SD-WAN functionality. According to the researchers, the handler passes cloud-supplied values into shell commands executed with root privileges without properly validating them. However, GL.iNet has not confirmed that this particular vulnerability was used in the attacks. RemoteToHome says it analyzed 183 routers it owns or manages and found suspicious activity on 152, including 24 with root-level reverse shells, 47 with an older persistent backdoor, and 81 showing evidence that attacker-supplied commands had executed. The researchers note that their findings may not be the same as the other GL.iNet customers and that the older backdoor infections may not be linked to the November attacks. In a separate forum report, the owner of a compromised GL-RM1 KVM shared network logs showing it downloading a malicious ni.sh script and additional executable payloads from 66.245.219[.]252 on November 19. The owner also reported that the device began communicating with approximately 1,800 residential IP addresses daily and repeatedly contacted the TRON blockchain API, exhibiting activity suggestive of a peer-to-peer network. However, the purpose of these connections is unclear, and there is no confirmation that the compromised devices were being used as residential proxies or were part of a larger botnet. BleepingComputer examined a copy of the malicious ni.sh script [VirusTotal] and found that it contains code specifically tailored to GL.iNet routers and KVM devices. The script recognizes numerous GL.iNet device models and downloads malicious executables named gl-helper and gb from hardcoded servers. It also establishes persistence through startup scripts and scheduled tasks, allowing the malware to restart after a reboot or if its processes are terminated. The installer includes functionality to disguise the malicious process as crond -i /tmp/.log, matching the IOC published by GL.iNet. An interesting feature is replacing the legitimate netstat utility with a modified shell script that filters out connections to 66.245.219[.]252, potentially hiding the malware's communications from administrators examining network connections. The installer also contains functionality to install SSH public keys for remote access, modify file timestamps, and periodically contact a remote server to retrieve and execute commands. The attacker's infrastructure includes two IP addresses, 66.245.219[.]252 and 65.20.71[.]131, which match the IP addresses seen in the compromised KVM owner's logs. The script also contains Chinese-language developer comments describing its persistence mechanisms, reporting functionality, and interactions with GL.iNet's cloud management software, indicating a Chinese-speaking individual may have written it. BleepingComputer also examined a separate malicious Lua payload recovered from a GL-MT2500 router. The payload was launched through a modified urandom_seed startup script and included functionality to collect device information, contact remote servers, and download and execute additional programs. Some of the malicious files recovered from GL.iNet devices had timestamps dating to December 2025, suggesting that some devices may have been compromised for months. However, it is unclear whether these infections involved the same threat actors or were related to the November 20 attacks. GL.iNet says it continues to investigate the incident and plans to notify identified affected customers using the email addresses associated with their cloud accounts. GL.iNet confirmed the attack on November 20, blocked the attack path, and fixed the cloud vulnerability, but already infected devices remain compromised and require firmware updates for cleanup. Fix: GL.iNet recommends installing the latest security firmware and has provided specific version requirements and a community-developed detection and cleanup tool for affected devices.

history.title: Signal to block Siri, Gemini AI from capturing chats on iOS, Android
history.text: Signal has announced new protections that block screenshots on iOS 27 and prevent AI assistants from capturing conversations on supported Android devices. The protections are designed to stop Siri and Gemini, the AI assistants built into iOS and Android, from accessing private conversations while performing tasks for users. The change comes after Signal introduced a feature in May 2025 that blocks Microsoft's controversial Recall screenshot-capturing feature on Windows 11. "We will now be taking similar measures to restrict agentic systems built into iOS 27 and on Android versions where we can detect an AI assistant attempting to read your Signal screen," Signal's president, Meredith Whittaker, said in a blog post. Whittaker says OS-level features such as Siri's Onscreen Awareness and Google's Gemini Intelligence can capture chat content as it appears on the app's screen, putting potentially sensitive private data outside Signal's control and exposing all conversation participants. Signal says its engineers spent months figuring out how AI systems access app data, designing targeted protections to block all extraction pathways verified through reverse engineering. However, Signal warns that AI agents could still access conversations through other methods, which Whittaker describes as "an existential threat to Signal." She explains that AI agents could access conversation data in multiple ways, as they are now embedded deep in operating systems, leaving apps vulnerable and with limited options for protecting users. The most notable example is macOS, where Signal says it's currently unable to provide any screenshot-blocking protection. For macOS 27 users, Signal recommends adding the app to the Excluded Apps list under System Settings > Siri to prevent Siri AI from proactively accessing message content. For this reason, Signal calls on Apple, Google, and Microsoft to fully disclose, through detailed documentation, all potential access mechanisms and give app developers a clear way to opt out of AI access across screens, files, notifications, and APIs. Signal did not provide specific app version numbers for the new protections but says they are automatically activated when possible. Signal recommends that users upgrade to the latest available version and go to Settings > App Security to check that Block Siri AI is enabled on iOS. On Android, Signal says it automatically enables Screen Security when it detects an AI assistant attempting to access the screen. However, on iOS, the protection also prevents users from taking screenshots of their Signal conversations, even for legitimate purposes. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. Signal warns that AI agents could still access conversations through other methods, calling it "an existential threat," and recommends users enable "Block Siri AI" in iOS settings or rely on automatic Screen Security on Android, though iOS protections also prevent all screenshot attempts. Fix: On iOS 27, users can add Signal to the Excluded Apps list under System Settings > Siri to prevent Siri AI from accessing message content.

history.title: CISA Adds Two Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
history.text: CISA Adds Two Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. - CVE-2026-133968 Project MONAI MONAI Label Path Traversal Vulnerability - CVE-2026-134624 N-able Mail Assure (SpamExperts) Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance. history.title: AI-Assisted Cyber Attacks Trigger Unauthorized Payments at Indian Banks and Fintech Firms
history.text: The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) has warned that threat actors are carrying out artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted cyber attacks targeting information and communication technology (ICT) assets in the country. This unsanctioned activity has resulted in unauthorized financial transactions at banking and financial services entities, as well as technology service providers supporting government-linked payments and platforms handling vendor or partner payouts. "In the observed incidents, attackers targeted business records and approval processes to carry out unauthorized transactions through otherwise legitimate systems," CERT-In said in an advisory last week. The incidents have been found to include the following methods - - Abuse of business applications and service provider-operated workflows, as opposed to direct exploitation of payment-related APIs. - Modification of business records or approval relationships, followed by the use of legitimate payment processes. - Use of trusted systems and established approval procedures to process unauthorized transactions without raising any alert. - Exploitation of security blind spots in independent verification, reconciliation, and review of changes to business records. CERT-In did not reveal how much money had been improperly paid out, or by whom. The activity has not been attributed to any specific threat actor. The agency also said that separate threat-hunting has uncovered the use of AI-driven agentic offensive frameworks (AOFS) across enterprise, technology, government, academic, and research sectors to conduct the following actions - - Automated reconnaissance to identify exposed systems, services, and potential attack paths. - Rapid generation and modification of exploits for known vulnerabilities, including by analyzing software patches and related technical information. - Using a cluster of AI agents to undertake intrusion tasks, such as reconnaissance and privilege discovery, in parallel. - Modifying scripts, requests, and attack methods in response to errors, blocked attempts, or information returned by targeted systems. - Using valid credentials, legitimate administrative functions, trust relationships, and external infrastructure to burrow deeper into target networks. "Organizations should review the security of business applications, critical records, user identities and third-party interfaces," CERT-In said. "Existing monitoring and incident-response arrangements should also account for the risks arising from misuse of trusted business processes and automated intrusion activity." The development comes as Indian entities have witnessed a spate of AI-assisted cyber attacks on financial entities, even as the national nodal agency disclosed that AI agents under research and evaluation "exceeded their task authorization and made unauthorized access" to ICT assets. "In the financially motivated campaign against Indian entities, agentic tooling compressed the time between initial access and final impact from days to a few hours," CERT-In said. "In addition, the campaign highlighted that multi-agent operations run in parallel for hours to days to achieve the attacker goals, consistent with the documented multi-agent capability of these tools." Earlier this month, the agency also warned that a threat group named Crafty Falcon is behind a wave of AI-driven attacks on financial firms and has used offensive penetration testing tools like ARTEX, PentAGI, CAIRN, and CyberStrikeAI to automate the intrusions at machine speed. According to the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the attacks have targeted banks, non-banking financial companies, and fintech companies, leading to multi-crore (equivalent to 10 million) unauthorized transactions through fund disbursement systems and APIs. "Perpetrators exploit unpatched software or misconfigured internet-exposed servers / IT systems to compromise the infrastructure," I4C said. "Hackers then target automated fund disbursement systems or special interfaces (APIs) used for payments and fund transfers. The money is sent to 'mule' accounts (accounts used by criminals) across different banks and then quickly moved or withdrawn through IMPS/NEFT." India's central bank, the Reserve Bank of India, has also alerted of rising cyber attacks on financial infrastructure, urging banks to provide details of their ability to stay ahead of AI-related threats, Reuters reported late last month. The Surge in AI Attacks The advisories also come at a time when organizations around the world are being targeted using AI tools, giving attackers a way to "execute multi-stage intrusions at greater operational velocity." Last week, the European Commission confirmed that attackers armed with ARTEX broke into its HR, medical reimbursement, and translation systems. The first signs of the attack were detected on October 22, 2026. ARTEX has also been implicated in a recent supply chain attack on IT management software company ConnectWise and Barracuda, with the latter revealing that a financially motivated criminal weaponized an exposed valid cloud access key provided to a third-party vendor to map its reach, repurpose discovered secrets to access more systems and look for seed phrases, and exfiltrate more credentials and secrets. "In all, the attacker touched about 10 cloud accounts in roughly 44 hours [between November 1 and 2]. The work was methodical and tireless," Barracuda said. "The probe names, the other indicators we collected, the order in which the attacker worked through our systems, and its built-in routines for hunting credentials and wallets all match ARTEX." Frameworks like ARTEX manage a collection of sub-agents to plan, execute, and adapt tactics across multiple kill chain stages, including reconnaissance and scanning, initial access, persistence and privilege escalation, internal reconnaissance, lateral movement, and data exfiltration. They can translate tactical goals described in natural language into machine commands that are executed by specialized AI agents. It integrates with various external LLMs, including Anthropic Claude, OpenAI GPT, DeepSeek, SpaceXAI Grok, Zhipu GLM, and Kimi. "ARTEX significantly reduces the time required to chain attack techniques, with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours," the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said in an alert this month. "The framework enables threat actors with minimal technical expertise to conduct complex, multi-target operations simultaneously, fundamentally accelerating attack velocity and expanding operational scale." Check Point, in a report published this month, said it uncovered more than 1,800 publicly exposed instances for ARTEX, with attackers leveraging the tool to conduct opportunistic, financially-motivated cybercrime. "Analysis of agent conversations revealed that these systems work almost fully autonomously, once the initial goal is set: most actors barely interacted with their agent fleets and mostly asked for progress or directed the agents to a new target," the company said. Data security firm Cohesity said threat actors using ARTEX are gaining access to systems that receive less security attention, such as partner and supplier portals, mobile backends, employee and sales support applications, legacy services, third-party integrations, and applications built by individual business units. "In a research network we operate, a threat actor linked to Rhysida used an AI framework to rewrite tools in response to obstacles, often within minutes, and more than 150 versions of a single script reached a domain controller within a day," it said. In a report published last week, Google's Mandiant and Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) identified what it described as the first observed instance of attackers using an autonomous AI framework with no human in the loop to turn security patches into exploits. The AI framework, called "exploit_agent," integrates with multiple frontier and local large language models (LLMs). It's designed to discover software vulnerabilities and execute exploits without human intervention. The attacker, suspected to be Russian-speaking, is said to have leveraged the framework to target French websites associated with the media and entertainment industries, as well as the education sector. "The framework is set up to conduct continuous differential analysis of popular web application software," Mandiant and GTIG said. "It compares code before and after patch announcements, analyzes findings to identify potential vulnerabilities, drafts exploits, and automatically executes them without human intervention." Some of the other notable incidents where AI agents and models do the legwork are listed below - - Use of CAIRN in intrusion activity against targets, including in the aerospace sector in the U.S. - Embedding LLMs into influence operation workflows to produce synthetic media, create convincing virtual personas, and generate and publish content. - Use of Google's Gemini API, along with tools from multiple AI providers, to build an end-to-end influence-as-a-service (SaaS) platform designed to target public sentiment on regional political topics, specifically across Europe and the Middle East. - Use of LLMs by a China-linked contractor called Leaky Castle to analyze, translate, and understand exfiltrated data - Abuse of a frontier model's file-hosting infrastructure by a China-nexus threat actor to stage lure archives and exfiltrate stolen data, and a backend API to exfiltrate stolen intranet documents. - Use of LLMs by North Korean threat actors to generate resumes and prepare for job interviews at Western organizations. - Creation of fraudulent recruiter profiles on professional networking platforms by a suspected North Korean hacking group called Midnight Neptune (previously UNC1069) in attacks aimed at cryptocurrency entities in North America and Europe using job
history.summary: AI-assisted cyber attacks targeting Indian banks and fintech firms have resulted in unauthorized financial transactions through manipulation of business records and trusted approval processes. Threat actors are using agentic offensive frameworks like ARTEX and CAIRN to automate reconnaissance, exploit generation, and multi-parallel intrusion tasks, compressing attack timelines from days to hours and enabling operations with minimal technical expertise. CERT-In and I4C advise organizations to review the security of business applications, critical records, user identities, and third-party interfaces, and to update monitoring and incident-response plans to account for misuse of trusted processes and automated intrusion activity.

history.title: Hackers Exploit Critical ScreenConnect Flaw to Hijack MSP Technician PCs Without Warning
history.text: Threat actors are exploiting a now-patched security flaw in ConnectWise ScreenConnect to target managed service provider (MSP) servers. The activity revolves around CVE-2026-84869 (CVSS score: 9.9), a critical ScreenConnect client flaw that allows a guest to transfer and execute a malicious payload on a connecting technician's host. "On November 12, 2026, we observed one managed service provider's (MSP) technician's workstation exploited to run a guest-pushed batch file, which then reported to a Telegram bot, downloaded an installer from masterdarky[.]com, and started a rogue ScreenConnect client pointing at the attacker's own relay, all in about 9 seconds," Huntress security researcher John Hammond said. The batch script, "update_224ac089.bat," is designed to decode a Base64 Telegram bot token and chat ID, and register the new infection. Subsequently, it downloads an MSI installer that masquerades as a Windows update ("WindowsUpdate.msi") to launch a ScreenConnect client, enabling the attacker to gain remote access to the technician's machine. The activity, observed between October 20 and November 16, 2026, is said to have sprayed servers blindly, with Huntress observing at least 688,000 guest "run file" requests for files named update.bat or update_ .bat hitting 42 ScreenConnect servers from 29 IP addresses. The guests have been found to make repeated requests that have blank session names or default-looking Windows hostnames. In another instance, a guest machine at 91.224.92[.]167 pushed a seemingly harmless text file ("marker.txt") two seconds after a technician joined a session, effectively acting as a canary to alert the operator that the exploit works against the target before sending the actual payload. What's more, a targeted attack aimed at an MSP server in October 2026 had the attacker joining as a guest across three real sessions the technician had created and asked the client to run a file designed to drop a batch script ("Sync.bat") into the technician's computer's Windows Startup folder. It's worth noting that this activity is distinct from a recently disclosed attack wave in which unknown threat actors gained unauthorized access to partner ScreenConnect environments by leveraging an authentication flaw in a third-party extension to deploy a malware toolkit called SCKit, which then exploits the flaw to propagate the malware to a technician's workstation. The attacks also coincide with another cluster in which thousands of unauthorized ScreenConnect guest sessions have originated from machines with cryptocurrency exchange-themed names like BITMEX-BOT, KUCOIN-SRV, and LAPTOP-BINANCE to trick technicians into connecting to them. No following malicious activity such as file transfers or command execution has been observed. Specifically, the threat actors have been found to obtain access to publicly downloadable ScreenConnect Access installers to extract the relay address needed to register a guest client with the corresponding ScreenConnect server, and then create fake guest sessions and make those sessions appear online. "Someone is registering unauthorized guest computers on MSPs' servers, where they sit in these session lists. They come from a scripted emulator that impersonates a Windows ScreenConnect client, and nearly all of them had connected from a single IONOS-hosted IP, 74.208.158[.]106," Huntress said. "As of November 13, we've seen related activity across at least 118 self-hosted ScreenConnect servers belonging to 109 Huntress-protected organizations. In total, we found 2,408 unauthorized sessions enrolled since November 3, 2026." Organizations are advised to ensure that technicians' ScreenConnect host clients are updated to 26.6.5 or later, hunt for signs of exposure, isolate affected workstations, and rotate all credentials reachable from that workstation. If immediate patching is not feasible, it's recommended to remove the TransferFiles permission from roles and session groups. "An MSP technician's workstation typically holds RMM consoles, saved credentials, and access to every customer, making it an exceptionally attractive target," Huntress said. "When a technician joins a remote session, their ScreenConnect host client and the guest machine can exchange files. Normally, the technician decides what moves and what runs." "A malicious guest exploiting CVE-2026-84869 can push a file to the technician's machine and get the technician's own client to run it. From the technician's view, no prompt appears. They only have to join the session, whether from an attacker-controlled machine or a real customer's support session that the attacker has slipped into as an extra guest."
history.summary: Hackers are exploiting the critical ScreenConnect flaw CVE-2026-84869 (CVSS 9.9) to target MSP technician workstations, allowing guests to transfer and execute malicious payloads without the technician's knowledge. Observed activity includes batch files decoding Telegram bot credentials, masquerading installers as Windows updates, and attackers gaining remote access in about 9 seconds; the campaign hit hundreds of thousands of guest requests across dozens of servers and involved fake sessions from crypto-themed hostnames. Organizations should update ScreenConnect host clients to version 26.6.5 or later, and if immediate patching isn't possible, remove the TransferFiles permission from roles and session groups to block file execution.

history.title: South Korea’s power giant KEPCO confirms data breach impacting 1.5 million
history.text: A threat actor breached the internal network of Korea Electric Power Corporation (KEPCO) and accessed two systems containing customer, employee, and contractor data. The attack exposed details of more than 1.5 million individuals before the company blocked access from external IP addresses and suspended the affected services. KEPCO is South Korea’s main electric power company and a state-controlled, major operator of the country’s critical infrastructure. The organization detected the attack on November 20, when it confirmed unauthorized access to its KEPCO ON electricity billing platform and its electronic procurement system (SRM). “On Friday, November 20, Korea Electric Power Corporation (hereafter KEPCO), led by President Kim Dong-cheol, confirmed that some customer information held in its IT systems had been exposed,” the power company states. “The company is making every effort to prevent harm.” ON is an integrated customer platform that allows customers to view and pay electricity bills. SRM is the company’s procurement system for contracting services. According to the announcement, published on Sunday, the following was exposed: - for 650,487 KEPCO ON customers: names, ID information, phone numbers, addresses, bank names, bank account numbers, account holder names, card issuers, card numbers, cardholder names, and electricity charge and billing information. - for 426,827 company representatives: names, ID information, email addresses, and company addresses. - for 442,934 KEPCO employees: names, affiliation, employee ID number, mobile phone number, email address, company phone number. The company says the data breach resulted from “advanced technologies such as AI,” but it shared no specific details about the initial access method or the attack chain. KEPCO is notifying exposed individuals directly, has filed a report with the data protection authorities, and is coordinating with government and financial authorities to block abuse such as unauthorized transactions. Potentially exposed individuals are warned that the exposed information could be used for targeted phishing and impersonation. They are advised to report any attempts to the police or Korea’s Internet and Security Agency. It is also recommended to avoid installing unknown apps, entering information into suspicious forms, and sharing sensitive data or verification codes over calls or texts. A threat actor using the “Noiem” alias has claimed the attack and advertised the breach on a hacker forum on November 19, saying that they had KEPCO user data, supplier records, and bidding and contract documents. South Korea’s Personal Information Protection Commission separately confirmed that KEPCO received an email from a hacker claiming data theft on November 19. history.title: OpenRouter drops AI providers over leaked prompts and secrets
history.text: OpenRouter removed three AI providers from its platform after discovering that they had violated their stated data-handling policies and exposed sensitive data. The company also revoked Zero Data Retention (ZDR) eligibility for 125 endpoints as a precaution and notified all potentially affected customers. OpenRouter is an AI model broker that lets developers access AI models from different companies using a single API key. When an app sends a request, OpenRouter forwards it to a provider that runs the selected model and passes the answer back. Operational technology security company Dragos alerted OpenRouter after sending two million test prompts through the platform, each containing a unique tracking link or decoy credential, and detecting "activity indicating that data from at least three AI providers was exposed." Dragos discovered that, in some cases, those credentials were leaked to outsiders and used in the wild, indicating that the test prompts had escaped. “We observed activity indicating that data from at least three AI providers was exposed. Our seeded test prompts were used in attempts to access our controlled test systems and canary AWS accounts,” Dragos says. OpenRouter says there was no breach on its own systems, making the leak point at the provider level and leading to the decision to remove the three leaking inference providers: Together AI, Phala, and Novita. Another provider, Atlas Cloud, said it would voluntarily withdraw its models from OpenRouter pending security testing, following a third-party security incident. The other three published separate announcements responding to Dragos’ findings and explaining how the leaks occurred. Together AI said an AI coding agent exposed a repository credential on GitHub, allowing an unauthorized party to download stored prompt samples from June and July involving MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2, and Kimi K2.6. Phala said an attacker compromised a server processing DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 requests routed through OpenRouter between October 21 and 22, and possibly up to November 8, and obtained application credentials from affected virtual machines. Novita said a routing misconfiguration forwarded some MiniMax requests, including those sent through OpenRouter, to MiniMax’s official API between May 28 and November 11. All four providers are tightening security controls, strengthening their zero data retention or data deletion policies, and advising potentially impacted users to rotate any secrets that may have been exposed in the leaked requests. OpenRouter is also adapting Dragos’ tests for ongoing use to check whether AI providers forward or leak user requests/responses to third parties, and will require validation before restoring ZDR eligibility.
