history.title: Microsoft Azure flaw exploited to steal customers' API credentials
history.text: Microsoft is warning customers that a security vulnerability in Azure API Management (APIM) Classic tiers was exploited to steal stored API credentials, with Norwegian authorities linking the flaw to cyberattacks against energy companies. Azure API Management is a cloud service that lets organizations publish, secure, monitor, and manage APIs that connect applications, services, and data. In an Azure Service Health security advisory (Tracking ID: MZK9-GH0) sent to customers and shared with BleepingComputer, Microsoft said it identified the vulnerability on November 18, 2026, and deployed a mitigation the following day. "Our investigation found that customers were exposed and an unauthorized party could have used the issue to access secrets stored in Azure API Management Classic instances before Microsoft identified the security issue," Microsoft said in the advisory. According to Microsoft, the vulnerability allowed unauthorized access to certain management functionality when APIM Classic instances were not configured according to recommended security best practices. This access could have allowed attackers to perform administrative operations, including accessing secrets stored in the service. Microsoft said the following information may have been exposed: - Secrets stored in Named Values - Client secrets associated with identity providers - Client secrets associated with OpenID Connect providers - Subscription keys - Tokens used to call direct management APIs These credentials could potentially allow attackers to access additional applications, services, or backend systems, depending on their permissions. Microsoft said it closed the unauthorized access path on November 19 and rotated Microsoft-controlled keys and credentials where appropriate. However, the company warned that its remediation would not invalidate customer credentials that may have been compromised before the fix was deployed. "This remediation blocks the unauthorized management-plane access path that could allow an actor to perform administrative operations, including secrets management, against Azure API Management services," Microsoft warned. "However, it does not automatically invalidate credentials that may have been accessed before the fix was deployed." The vulnerability affects Azure API Management Classic tiers, while Microsoft said APIM v2 tiers are not impacted. Microsoft urged affected customers to immediately rotate potentially exposed credentials, investigate suspicious activity in systems accessible through those credentials, and review available logs for signs of unauthorized access. In a Reddit post, an administrator claimed their organization discovered the vulnerability after detecting unauthorized access to Azure Key Vault using a valid administrator token. "Our company has been fighting this for days, after discovering that someone logged into our keyvaults using a valid administrator token and not following the normal access pattern," the administrator claimed. The administrator alleged that attackers exploited a zero-day authentication bypass in a deprecated legacy API to gain access to a privileged system account on APIM instances. According to the administrator, the legacy API did not generate logs that customers could use to detect the unauthorized access. They also alleged that Microsoft initially attributed the suspicious activity to leaked customer credentials before deploying a global fix. BleepingComputer has not independently verified these allegations. The vulnerability has also been linked to attacks affecting Norwegian organizations, including energy companies Equinor and Skagerak Energi. In a security advisory, Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) said an unknown threat actor targeted access tokens, secrets, and named values stored in Azure API Management. The agency said Norway's energy sector first discovered the vulnerability and that organizations in other countries and industries were also affected. Equinor disclosed an ongoing cyberattack on November 17, a day before Microsoft says it identified the APIM vulnerability. The company later announced that it had stopped the attack and found no indication that data had been stolen or altered. Skagerak Energi also reported an attempted cyberattack but said it had no impact on its operations and no evidence that information was compromised. While Microsoft says it deployed a remediation on November 19 that required no customer action, NSM's advisory warns organizations to verify that their APIM instances have received the security update. The agency warns that instances running below specific runtime versions remain vulnerable and advises customers to contact their "service provider" if they have not received the update. It is unclear whether the runtime updates are separate from Microsoft's initial mitigation. Cloud security researcher Anders Kristiansen shared threat-hunting queries to help organizations investigate potential exploitation and identify credentials stored in their APIM instances. BleepingComputer contacted Microsoft with questions about the attacks but has not received a reply yet. This Azure API Management incident comes just days after Microsoft confirmed another security breach involving its Entra Connect Health service, where attackers exploited a vulnerability to steal tenant configuration information and administrator email addresses. The flaw was identified on November 18, 2026, and a mitigation was deployed the next day, but the remediation does not invalidate credentials that may have been compromised before the fix. history.title: Spanish LaLiga confirms hackers stole soccer fans’ personal data
history.text: LaLiga, Spain's top men's professional football league, disclosed a data breach that exposed personal information belonging to users of its services and those of some affiliated clubs. According to the organization, the incident occurred between November 14 and 16, and the attacker extracted data from compromised systems. LaLiga organizes Spain’s top two men’s professional football divisions. The top league is one of the world’s most prominent football leagues, where clubs with a global audience, such as Real Madrid, FC Barcelona, and Atlético Madrid, play. On November 16, the organization’s security team identified the source of the unauthorized access and implemented measures to block the attack and stop the data extraction. “LALIGA was the target of a cyberattack on one of its technology platforms for fan services,” reads the announcement. “Between November 14 and 16, a cybercriminal gained unauthorized access to the platform and extracted personal data belonging to users registered for digital services offered by LALIGA and some clubs.” LaLiga underlined that the incident was confined to a specific platform and did not extend to other systems that support the running of the competitions. After implementing containment measures, LaLiga launched an investigation to determine the scope of the incident and introduced more thorough monitoring to detect future attempts to breach its systems. The football organizer also reported the incident to the Spanish Data Protection Agency (AEPD) and filed a complaint with the National Police’s Central Cybercrime Unit. Impacted clubs were also directly notified, and actions to inform impacted fans are being coordinated. At the time of writing, no ransomware group has claimed responsibility for the attack on LaLiga. BleepingComputer has contacted the organization to learn more about the attack and which clubs were impacted, but we have not received a response as of publication. history.title: GlobeTopper loses $2.5 million after hackers steal $70k in gift cards
history.text: A cyberattack disrupted operations at B2B top-up solutions provider GlobeTopper, causing an estimated $2.5 million in lost revenue, while the attacker redeemed digital gift cards worth $70,000. Parent company iQSTEL said that the intrusion was detected on October 22 and GlobeTopper responded by suspending its platform and starting an investigation. GlobeTopper is a business-to-business digital gift card distributor. Various retailers, fintech apps, and rewards platforms use its API. According to the platform’s website, it is used by more than 4,000 brands across 65 countries, including IKEA, Adidas, Spotify, Target, and Roblox. In a filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), iQSTEL said that GlobeTopper detected more unauthorized activity the day after it identified the attack. In response, the company "took the platform and all affected servers offline" in the early hours of October 23 to investigate and fix the problem. The company deployed a completely rebuilt platform on AWS on October 31, while commercial operations were restored in stages, starting November 1. GlobeTopper says the attacker obtained certain client API credentials and integration keys, which have been revoked and replaced, and it has observed no unauthorized use of them yet. “During its investigation, the Company determined that the unauthorized party obtained API credentials and integration keys of certain GlobeTopper business customers,” iQSTEL says. “All affected credentials and integration keys have been revoked and rotated, and affected business customers have been issued new credentials subject to additional access restrictions.” The company further stated that an investigation is ongoing to determine whether other customer, personal, payment, or provider data was accessed or acquired. Regarding the digital gift cards the attackers redeemed, the company says it cannot block, recover, or reclaim them, and will incur the losses. iQSTEL said the incident hurt GlobeTopper’s fourth-quarter transaction volume and operating results, but as of the filing, it has not determined it to be material. BleepingComputer has emailed iQSTEL with additional questions regarding the incident, but the company declined to share further information. At the time of writing, no ransomware groups have listed iQSTEL or GlobeTopper as victims on their extortion portals. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. history.title: AI Inference Providers Failed to Detect Hacking and Prompt Theft, Says Dragos
history.text: Threat actors breached at least three AI inference providers and stole customer prompts, but none detected the intrusions until they were notified, according to cybersecurity firm Dragos. AI inference providers host AI models and sell access to them through APIs. The hacks were detected after a team led by Dragos chief research officer HD Moore sent out roughly two million prompts to widely used AI services between July and November. These prompts contained a unique, trackable bait such as URLs, hostnames, and credentials, including AWS keys. The security firm then set up a monitoring system to see whether anyone used the bait information in the wild, which meant the prompt had been compromised. Dragos soon found evidence indicating that someone had stolen information from one of the tested AI inference providers. “Although our prompts were bait, they were processed along with real customer requests, and those were almost certainly copied too,” Moore noted. The biggest breach involved roughly 200 AWS test keys sent to a provider, which were stolen in late October. “Some of the stolen keys came from requests that the provider rejected before a model ever ran – this tells us that the attacker was copying requests at the provider’s front door, and not somewhere deeper in the inference stack,” Moore said. Dragos saw the attackers checking which stolen keys worked, then trying to use them to obtain valuable data from the associated accounts. The attackers have not been identified, but Dragos said one adversary appears to have hacked two of the providers at the same time, using secrets stolen from both from a single rented server. OpenRouter, an AI gateway that sends customer requests to dozens of inference providers, was indirectly affected. The company said its own systems were not breached, but it removed three unnamed providers in response to the incident. OpenRouter also listed security notices published by several providers. It did not say whether these are among the three it removed. The list includes confidential AI cloud provider Phala, which said an attacker compromised a server running a DeepSeek model served via OpenRouter. It admitted that requests sent between October 21 and November 8 should be considered exposed. AI cloud platform Together AI revealed that an AI coding agent leaked credentials on GitHub, which were then used to obtain stored prompt samples. Model hosting platform Novita and inference platform Atlas Cloud traced potential exposure to requests that reached the API of model developer MiniMax. history.summary: Threat actors breached at least three AI inference providers and stole customer prompts without detection until notified, according to Dragos. The firm embedded unique trackable bait—including URLs, hostnames, and AWS keys—in roughly two million prompts sent to AI services between July and November, then monitored for wild use to confirm compromise. One breach involved roughly 200 AWS test keys stolen from a provider in late October, with attackers later verifying the keys and attempting to access associated account data.

history.title: BadBox 3.0 Ad Fraud Operation Generating 40 Billion Daily Bid Requests Disrupted
history.text: Bot and fraud protection firm Human Security says it has disrupted the largest ad fraud botnet by bid volume. Dubbed BadBox 3.0, it is the third iteration of a large operation targeting low-cost Android devices. The first BadBox botnet ensnared more than 190,000 devices, while BadBox 2.0 was initially found on over 1 million devices, but eventually ensnared more than 10 million. “At its height, BadBox 3.0 accounted for roughly 40 billion bid requests a day and more than 4% of all CTV traffic observed by the Human Defense Platform,” Human Security says, noting the bid request volume was three times the volume recorded for the VastFlux ad fraud scheme. Portions of BadBox 3.0, the cybersecurity firm says, were operated via command-and-control (C&C) domains that were disrupted when Google took down XCPE, a botnet of over 1.3 million Android set-top boxes. The botnet consists of low-cost, uncertified Android Open Source Project devices infected with backdoors delivering fraud modules designed to render hidden video ads and to enroll the devices into residential proxy networks. Human Security says its Satori Threat Intelligence and Research Team has uncovered an actively maintained catalog of fraud modules hosted on public repositories, as well as links to Chinese electronics manufacturer TXCZ. Some of the modules were previously seen in BadBox and BadBox 2.0. “Most modules in the catalog are residential proxy modules and the droppers that install them, but the collection also carries new ad fraud modules, and researchers traced both payloads to the same infrastructure and code,” Human Security notes. Mimicking video ad software development kits (SDKs), the botnet’s ad fraud modules render ads in a hidden window, making the bid requests appear as coming from known, legitimate apps that the threat actors impersonated. While the device owner does not see the ads, the supply chain sees a premium CTV inventory consisting of well-known applications that likely aren’t even installed on the infected devices, along with residential IP addresses and full video ads. In some cases, the threat actors relied on server-side ad insertion (SSAI) to monetize application spoofing. “The volume reached roughly 40 billion bid requests a day, and much of it arrived from IP addresses associated with residential proxy networks, which helped it pass as ordinary household viewing,” Human Security notes. Proxyjacking modules deployed on the same devices enrolled them in eleven residential proxy networks, including a rebranded version of IpMoYu, now named PXYEDGE, the network operated by the threat actors behind BadBox and BadBox 2.0. Human Security has found several links between BadBox 3.0 and the Chinese company TXCZ: the modules check for TXCZ build properties, a TXCZ domain serves payload download routes and configurations for the hidden ads, and Human linked TXCZ to repositories distributing ad fraud launchers. In addition to public repositories, the threat actor uses a second code platform and a file server to host payloads. For some payloads, it also uses a free open-source CDN that mirrors public repositories. The operators also use a self-hosted GitHub proxy. Human Security has not provided an estimated size of BadBox 3.0, but noted that the mirror for one repository served over 367,000 requests over a month, which does not reflect the number of infections. “These are requests rather than unique devices, and some come from researchers and scanners. It should be made very clear: these numbers are only for one repository, and only of the third backup delivery mechanism. The actual number of BADBOX 3.0 infections can be presumed to be significantly higher,” the cybersecurity firm notes. history.title: Check Point Security Management Servers Hacked in AI-Assisted Campaign
history.text: A threat actor has been using AI-enabled offensive tools in a broad campaign targeting Check Point Security Management servers, threat intelligence firm GreyNoise reports. As part of the campaign, which the security firm started tracking in early October and is likely still ongoing, a threat actor tracked as GreyNoise Threat 13 (GT13) has been conducting scanning, exploitation, and control activities from 99 IP addresses, many associated with disposable network infrastructure. According to GreyNoise, GT13 targeted at least 22 organizations from the energy, engineering, financial services, government, manufacturing, mining, and transportation sectors across the US, the UK, Australia, Austria, China, France, Germany, Hong Kong, the Netherlands, South Korea, and other geographies. GreyNoise believes the threat actor has been using agentic harnesses and systems to weaponize vulnerabilities, find vulnerable assets, and automatically exploit them. The automated operations were complemented by hands-on-keyboard activity. “We witnessed the GT13 actor use 99 IP addresses, all of which were either egresses through ExpressVPN or compromised victim Check Point devices, including activity over 1400+ network sessions, 800+ command line artifacts, and 1200+ files downloaded, uploaded, or created,” GreyNoise says. In one instance, GreyNoise tracked the activity to October 2, when the threat actor forged a signed admin session cookie to gain administrative access to an HFS server. The attacker obtained SSH access to the server, which was used to scan the environment and exfiltrate data. “The GT13 adversary had access to the victim Check Point Security Management servers before they compromised the HFS server. We could not determine when or how the attacker gained access to those Check Point assets,” the company notes. The attacker deployed tools such as Nmap, Chisel, Impacket, Paramiko, and other Python utilities and scripts, performed reconnaissance, lateral movement, and privilege escalation. They used one victim’s server as a hop to save command results and data exfiltrated from 24 previously compromised Check Point Security Management servers. Between October 20 and 26, in addition to gaining deeper access to the victim’s environment, the threat actor conducted bulk actions against 21 other victim Check Point devices. GT13 issued a bulk certificate-management task to 24 servers across the 22 organizations. The task failed, but the threat actor collected the responses on the relay server in text files. “These files contained the victim IP addresses and were in incrementing IP order, indicating an automation looped through them to run the commands on the compromised Check Point servers and deliver them via scp to this exfil folder. Each file was delivered from victim infrastructure, showing that each of the compromised devices holds the SSH private key that matches the public key planted on the hop,” GreyNoise says. The activity within the first victim’s environment also involved the use or attempted exploitation of vulnerabilities such as CVE-2026-61500 (Rejetto HFS), CVE-2023-4966 and CVE-2025-5777 (Citrix NetScaler), CVE-2024-21893 (Ivanti), CVE-2026-16232 (Check Point SmartConsole), CVE-2026-98432 (Linux IPv4 UAF), CVE-2020-1472 and CVE-2026-41089 (Windows NetLogon), CVE-2021-26855 and CVE-2021-34473 (Microsoft Exchange), and CVE-2021-21972 and CVE-2023-34048 (VMware vCenter). GreyNoise says it confirmed threat actor activity against Check Point Security Management servers between October 17 and November 2, when it stopped observing it. However, the company believes the campaign is still ongoing as GT13 had persistent access to the compromised servers. “We believe the actor has separate agentic harnesses and systems weaponizing vulnerabilities, scanning for vulnerable assets, and automatically exploiting them to gather sets of systems that can be later used for operational relays or true targets. We suspect some of the foibles in the timeline reflect agentic offensive operations,” GreyNoise notes. history.summary: A threat actor tracked as GT13 has been using AI-enabled offensive tools to scan, exploit, and gain persistent access to Check Point Security Management servers from 99 IP addresses linked to disposable infrastructure, targeting at least 22 organizations across multiple sectors and geographies. The campaign involved automated exploitation of numerous vulnerabilities such as CVE-2026-61500, CVE-2023-4966, CVE-2025-5777, CVE-2024-21893, CVE-2026-16232, CVE-2026-98432, CVE-2020-1472, CVE-2026-41089, CVE-2021-26855, CVE-2021-34473, CVE-2021-21972, and CVE-2023-34048, combined with hands-on-keyboard activity including forged admin session cookies, SSH access, and data exfiltration via compromised relay servers.

history.title: Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA Series
history.text: Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA Series Summary Successful exploitation of this vulnerability could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code with webserver privileges. The following versions of Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA Series are affected: - AK-SM8xxA <=5.4.0 (CVE-2026-129713) Background - Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Commercial Facilities - Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide - Company Headquarters Location: Denmark Vulnerabilities Acknowledgments - Carlo Meijer of Midnight Blue reported CVE-2026-129713 to CISA. Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. - Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. - Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. - When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks: - Do not click web links or open attachments in unsolicited email messages. - Refer to Recognizing and Avoiding Email Scams for more information on avoiding email scams. - Refer to Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks for more information on social engineering attacks. No known public exploitation specifically targeting these vulnerabilities has been reported to CISA at this time. history.title: Hackers Exploit N-able MailAssure Flaw While AI Agents Exploit MONAI Label Zero-Day
history.text: The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Monday added two flaws impacting N-able MailAssure and MONAI Label to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing evidence of active exploitation. The critical vulnerabilities are listed below - - CVE-2026-134624 (CVSS score: 9.3) - A server-side request forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in N-able MailAssure's LDAP synchronization connection check that could allow an authenticated API user to connect to arbitrary internal hosts and ports, determine which are reachable, and send crafted data to internal services. - CVE-2026-133968 (CVSS score: 9.8) - A path traversal vulnerability in MONAI Label that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to write arbitrary files outside the intended datastore directory, potentially resulting in remote code execution. The exploitation of CVE-2026-134624 stems from a disclosure last week, in which N-able said it detected a security incident that resulted in a service disruption affecting Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud on November 16, 2026. As of November 21, 2026, 11:44 p.m. UTC, access to the Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud dashboard and APIs has been restored. "N-able has remediated the recent security incident affecting our Mail Assure and SpamExperts environments and restored the impacted functionality," a spokesperson for the company told The Hacker News. Our investigation to date indicates that exploitation was confined to a single N-able hosted server and continued monitoring since remediation has found no further malicious activity." CVE-2026-133968, on the other hand, has been linked to an agentic attack in which a suspected China-nexus threat actor leveraged CAIRN, an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered problem-solving engine, to conduct hacking operations with minimal human involvement. The activity, which ran for an approximately 48-hour period beginning September 8, 2026, targeted IP addresses associated with universities across East Asia outside mainland China. "In this campaign, the actor provided a list of targeted IP addresses with variations of the goal to 'obtain shell access,'" CJ Moses, CISO of Amazon Integrated Security, said. "Based on those inputs, the AI agents planned, executed, and adjusted their approach as they learned, without the operator choosing each next step." Some of these attacks unsuccessfully attempted to brute-force their way into a Redis instance at one university and a GPU server at another. The activity also singled out an unspecified target running MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging AI application, identifying the aforementioned zero-day and exploiting it in about 11 minutes to write arbitrary files to the server. "In a later session, the agents used the same vulnerability to write a Python reverse shell payload to sitecustomize.py, a file Python automatically imports at interpreter startup," Moses said. "The agents then triggered a training API endpoint to spawn a new Python process. The new process imported the payload and established a reverse shell running as root." Following the discovery of the zero-day, the operator is said to have provided the AI agents with a proxy to tunnel into a second university network running the same vulnerable software, and then directed them to target other machines in that network. The attacks are part of a broader cluster of attacks involving the use of AI-driven frameworks like ARTEX, CAIRN, and AntiFox, and CyberStrikeAI in recent months. A subset of these activities is estimated to have breached over 100 companies, including John Deere and SharkNinja. The end goals, per NorForge, revolve around establishing persistent access and financial theft - - AIA0001, which has targeted organizations, mainly in the U.S., Japan, and Australia, to deploy web shells and gain access to e-commerce and payment infrastructure for subsequent monetization. - AIA0002, which has targeted merchant payment services, gray-market payment sites, pharmaceutical sites, and a criminal carding site for financial gain. - AIA0003, which has targeted smaller e-commerce sites and very large U.S.-based commercial platforms to obtain shell access, admin panel access, or database access. In a report published last week, Amazon Web Services (AWS) also revealed that its MadPot sensor network captured requests from AI agents linked to two offensive campaigns running on ARTEX, an AI-native penetration framework. "The most prominent ARTEX campaign was a large-scale theft of credentials to access AI models, organized as a self-sustaining operation in which stolen keys paid for the LLM inference powering further credential hunting," AWS said. "Another campaign targeted cryptocurrency exchanges for know-your-customer (KYC) verification bypass using real-time deepfake injection." According to Datadog Security Labs, ARTEX also appears under other names like ScopeWeaver, LUCK — 自主资产控制台 (LUCK — Autonomous Asset Console), and 观澜SEC渗透测试平台 (Guanlan SEC Penetration Testing Platform). In-the-wild activity involving ARTEX has also targeted several AWS environments with an aim to access financial data. Initial access vectors used in these attacks include compromised long-term AWS access keys and public Cognito user pools, with the latter being used to register an account, collect tokens, and enumerate AWS accounts. "In one instance using a valid long-term access key, ARTEX's most frequent action was FilterLogEvents," security researcher Julie Agnes Sparks said. "The most common searches were various naming conventions of cryptocurrency companies, hedge funds, and related financial institutions. The terms combine a company name with words like fund, invoice, billing, and LLC." Telemetry data gathered by Previdian from its sensors has recorded 52 HTTP requests containing explicit ARTEX markers between October 18 and November 15, 2026, from 10 source IP addresses. "Further investigation of these sources identified 3,651 related HTTP records involving application discovery, authentication probing, remote code execution attempts, path traversal and attempts to retrieve sensitive configuration data," Ryan Dewhurst, founder and CEO of Previdian, said. "The most significant activity targeted Oracle WebLogic, Langflow, and Flowise, with additional payloads associated with Apache Struts, Log4j, and PHPUnit." Interestingly, one of the IP addresses associated with ARTEX activity, 31.22.91[.]156, overlaps with the AWS-documented campaign targeting AI infrastructure, including Langflow exploitation attempts consistent with CVE-2025-3248. In light of active exploitation, Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies are recommended to apply the latest fixes for the two flaws by November 26, 2026.

history.title: Schneider Electric EcoStruxure Power Build Rapsody software
history.text: Schneider Electric EcoStruxure Power Build Rapsody software Summary Schneider Electric is aware of a vulnerability in its EcoStruxure™ Power Build Rapsody product. The EcoStruxure™ Power Build Rapsody is used to enter or import the single line diagram, to get the extensive bill of material of your switchboard, including all devices, connection items, and mounting components. history.title: VMware Updates Patch Critical ESX, vCenter Vulnerabilities
history.text: Broadcom on Tuesday announced the release of patches for 23 vulnerabilities across multiple VMware products, including critical-severity flaws in ESX and vCenter. The vCenter patches resolve seven bugs, including a critical authentication bypass issue in the VMware Directory Service tracked as CVE-2026-123903 (CVSS score of 9.8). Additionally, the fixes target three denial-of-service (DoS) issues in the VMware Directory Service, a local privilege escalation in a vpxd service script, an arbitrary file write while processing certain archives, and a security policy enforcement failure in the vSphere Distributed Switch (vDS). The ESX updates resolve seven security issues as well, including three critical-severity weaknesses leading to code execution on the host. CVE-2026-123910 and CVE-2026-123911 (CVSS score of 9.8) are heap out-of-bounds write and use-after-free flaws in the I/O filter service, while CVE-2026-123912 (CVSS score of 9.3) is an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the XHCI USB controller that requires local administrative privileges on a virtual machine. An attacker “may exploit this issue to execute code as the virtual machine’s VMX process running on the host. On ESX, the exploitation is contained within the VMX sandbox whereas, on Workstation and Fusion, this may lead to code execution on the machine where Workstation or Fusion is installed,” Broadcom explains. The remaining four include a stack-based buffer overflow in the VMkernel, a DoS vulnerability in guest RPC, a security bypass in the host configuration store, and a signature verification bypass. Broadcom also patched eight flaws in Avi Load Balancer that could lead to code execution with root privileges, privilege escalation to root, command execution, password hash leaks, access to the routing management interface and other resources, and unintended file access, and one in VMware Tools leading to DoS. According to Broadcom, some of the issues were resolved with the vCenter updates released last week. vCenter version 8.0 U3m contained the fixes, and customers who applied it do not need to update again. vCenter 9.1.x deployments, however, as well as ESX, VMware Tools, Workstation, Fusion, and Avi Load Balancer instances, need to be updated. “Patches are cumulative, so the updates listed in this advisory also contain the fixes from VMSA-2026-0009 when they are newer than the fixed versions listed in VMSA-2026-0009. However, this advisory does not mention the SDDC Manager updates from VMSA-2026-0009; please ensure you are handling those,” the company notes. Broadcom makes no mention of any of these vulnerabilities being exploited in the wild, but it’s not uncommon for the company to not warn about exploitation in its public advisories. On Tuesday, Broadcom also updated its advisory on Node2Shell to add VMware Cloud Foundation version 9.1.2 to the list of fixed releases. history.title: CISA Adds Three Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
history.text: CISA Adds Three Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog CISA has added three new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. - CVE-2026-131914 Idunno AntiCsrf Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability - CVE-2026-132165 Drupal Core Remote Code Execution Vulnerability - CVE-2026-132224 Optimizely Web Experimentation External Control of Critical State Data Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance. history.title: An Unclassified CIA System Was Breached in a Cyberattack, AP Source Says
history.text: An unclassified CIA system was breached in a cyberattack, according to a person familiar with the incident who spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity. The breach did not involve any classified information and the issue has been resolved, said the person, who was not authorized to speak by name and spoke on condition of anonymity. The breach affected a system that handles open source intelligence, which involves the collection and analysis of publicly available data from sources including the internet, commercial satellites and private data brokers. Though the information is generally public or semi-public, open-source information can give intelligence analysts significant insight on its own or in combination with intelligence obtained from classified spying programs. It was not clear what specific information was compromised or who was responsible. The breach was first reported by The New York Times on Tuesday. The incident comes to light following a series of highly disruptive system failures that unnerved many Americans. An internal network the National Security Agency uses to communicate classified information was offline for a time last week, and the FBI is investigating an apparent hack of a national law enforcement database that it maintains. Those incidents followed a nationwide ground stop that snarled air travel after air traffic controllers struggled to communicate with pilots. Apple, JP Morgan Chase and Microsoft also had systems go down this month. The incidents have put a spotlight on the vulnerabilities inside critical infrastructure, banking systems and the digital tools that millions of people use daily. President Donald Trump’s administration says the series of outages is not part of a coordinated cyberattack and dispatched Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton to calm Americans in appearances on Sunday morning news shows. Clayton said the outages largely stem from the rush to patch and upgrade systems to stay ahead of hackers who are now empowered with sophisticated artificial intelligence tools to attack at an unprecedented scale. Related: FBI Investigating Apparent Hack of Its Key National Criminal Justice Database, AP Source Says
history.summary: Unclassified CIA system breached in cyberattack; breach did not involve classified information and the issue has been resolved. System handles open source intelligence involving publicly available data from internet, commercial satellites and private data brokers. Specific information compromised or responsible party not identified. Fix: Issue has been resolved.

history.title: Rackspace shuts down Spot cloud platform after security breach
history.text: Rackspace is shutting down its Rackspace Spot cloud platform after a security breach allowed hackers to access customer Kubernetes clusters and secrets, giving customers until December 8 to migrate their services and download their data. Rackspace Spot is a cloud platform that allows organizations to deploy and manage containerized applications using Kubernetes. The company announced the shutdown in a new security notification sent to customers and obtained by BleepingComputer, saying it had decided to discontinue the service after reviewing the incident. "Following a review of the situation, Rackspace has made the decision to wind down the Rackspace Spot service. This decision is being made to provide a clear path forward for customers," reads the notification. Rackspace says the service will be permanently discontinued on December 8, 2026, at 5 PM Central Time, when all remaining workloads will be terminated, and customer data will no longer be accessible. Customers have been instructed to retrieve their data and migrate their workloads to different platforms before the deadline. The decision comes after hackers breached Rackspace Spot on November 17 using compromised credentials, allowing them to create unauthorized pods in customer Kubernetes clusters, read Kubernetes Secrets, and list nodes and volumes. Rackspace discovered the intrusion on November 18 following a customer report and disabled access to the platform's administration console while securing its infrastructure. Service was restored on November 21 following an extended outage. "An unauthorized party gained access to parts of the Spot platform and may have read cluster Secrets and files on storage volumes," Rackspace said. The company says the affected Spot environment is segmented from its core infrastructure and that it has not identified evidence of unauthorized access to its core systems or the environments of other Rackspace customers. Rackspace is now instructing all Spot customers to treat their API tokens, refresh tokens, kubeconfigs, and Kubernetes Secrets as potentially compromised, regardless of whether they previously received a breach notification. Customers have also been advised to review access logs dating back to November 16 and search for suspicious Kubernetes objects associated with the attack, including: - IP address: 23.224.79.106 - IP range: 23.224.0.0/15 - Suspicious Kubernetes pod and object prefixes: i1, glm-, and probe Customers urge Rackspace to reconsider The shutdown announcement has prompted disappointment among Rackspace Spot customers, with some urging the company to reconsider and offering to pay more to keep the platform operational. In a Reddit discussion, one customer said they believed users would be willing to pay higher prices to keep the service running. Other customers expressed similar concerns in a separate discussion, with some asking about affordable alternatives and others describing the impact the shutdown would have on their existing infrastructure. Others praised the service for its affordability, saying alternative cloud providers would be more expensive. Rackspace has not indicated whether it will reconsider the shutdown decision or offer customers additional time to migrate their workloads. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. history.title: New Inception extortion gang launches large-scale vishing campaign
history.text: A newly formed data extortion group named ‘Inception’ has been linked to a large-scale campaign that targets single sign-on (SSO) credentials of multiple global brands and firms. The gang surfaced on November 17, claiming seven victims on its extortion site, including chip maker AMD, PepsiCo, Cigna Healthcare, AutoZone, and Lucid Motors, but none of them have publicly confirmed a data breach. However, cybersecurity company ReversingLabs has been tracking Inception gang's activity and says that it has been operating since late October. The security firm has confirmed the existence of 21 domains used for SSO phishing, 41 domains believed to be used in campaign infrastructure, and 4 other domains with suspected use. The researchers identified an extensive phishing infrastructure impersonating dozens of major corporations, including Dropbox, Duolingo, Western Union, Indeed, Activision Blizzard, Riot Games, Twitch, Reddit, Nestlé, Anthropic, Nintendo, Starbucks, McDonald's, Paramount, and NBCUniversal. The existence of these domains is not proof that those firms have been breached, or even targeted yet, and none have recently disclosed cyberattacks or other related incidents. The campaign appears to rely on phone-based social engineering rather than email phishing, strongly resembling the tactics used by the infamous ShinyHunters extortion group. Inception is using legal-themed websites that imitate corporate authentication services, primarily Okta but also NetIQ/OpenText Access Manager. ShinyHunters link and denial One of those authentication providers, Okta, published a report yesterday linking Inception to O-UNC-053, a threat cluster it previously associated with ShinyHunters, which has been active since March. According to Okta, after law enforcement disrupted the ShinyHunters extortion group following the arrest of suspected members [1, 2], and the shutdown of the leak site, O-UNC-053 continued to register new phishing domains. In late October, the activity cluster launched its legal-themed campaign, and in mid-November, the Inception leak site went live, announcing victims that matched previous targeting. “This gap in publishing on any leak site followed by publishing on a new data leak site with a new brand is consistent with prior shifts from Com-affiliated actors,” describes Okta. “Before and after the change in DLS publication, O-UNC-053 maintained consistent infrastructure and TTPs, leading us to assess that the cluster has very likely changed their brand affiliation.” Inception was quick to respond and dispute the alleged links to other threat actors in an announcement on their extortion page. The threat actors claimed to operate independently and with no affiliation to any previous group, arguing that overlapping targets and the use of common domain registration and CDN services did not establish operational links. They also acknowledged that private tooling is circulating among independent threat actors, and using it does not prove affiliation. To defend against the latest Inception campaign, ReversingLabs recommends enforcing phishing-resistant authentication, including FIDO2 security keys and passkeys, and strengthening help desk identity verification procedures. DNS, proxy, and identity provider logs dating back to October 21, 2026, should be carefully reviewed for signs of suspicious activity. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. history.title: Drupal Fail2Install Exploit Details Emerge as Critical RCE Flaw Faces Active Exploitation
history.text: The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Tuesday added a critical flaw impacting Drupal to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, requiring federal agencies to apply the fixes by November 27, 2026. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-132165 aka Fail2Install (CVSS score: 9.8), is a case of remote code execution (RCE) impacting Drupal core. "Drupal Core contains a not failing securely vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to take over an existing site or execute arbitrary code via the Drupal installer," CISA said. "Under specific conditions, the attacker can use install.php to attempt to reinstall Drupal on the site." As previously reported by The Hacker News, an attacker can use the installer to attempt to reinstall Drupal, resulting in site takeover or remote code execution under certain circumstances. According to an independent analysis by Searchlight Cyber, it has emerged that ordinary server resource limits can be abused to trick Drupal into mistakenly believing that an existing website was not installed, enter its installation process via "install.php," create an administrator-controlled account, and execute arbitrary PHP code. While Drupal has checks in place to determine whether the website is already installed before allowing installation to proceed, the research found that it's possible to bypass these checks by exhausting server resources. As a result, a failed database connection to the configured database and a failed database check for an existing installation are interpreted as evidence that the website has not been installed, and Drupal allows the installation to proceed after winning a race condition that allows a second database connectivity check to pass. To achieve this, the three resource exhaustion techniques have been put to use - - EMFILE, which refers to a limit on how many files a Linux process can open - Database connection exhaustion - TCP source-port exhaustion "We started with EMFILE, then explored database and TCP limits to determine whether availability failures could become security primitives," the cybersecurity company said. "Applying this methodology to Drupal uncovered a pre-authentication RCE affecting Drupal 8.9, 9, 10, and 11 across four common deployment combinations: Apache with PostgreSQL, Apache with MySQL, PHP-FPM with PostgreSQL, and PHP-FPM with MySQL." This behavior can be turned into a pathway for code execution by taking advantage of the fact that Drupal's installer supports SQLite database files and allows the database path to be selected during installation. This is made possible because the installer doesn't restrict the file name extension. "By selecting a path ending in .php under the document root, the installer creates an SQLite database with a PHP extension," Searchlight Cyber said. "Once the installation reaches the site configuration form, Drupal stores the submitted website name inside the SQLite database. By using PHP code as the website name, the payload bytes are written into the .php database file." While direct access to the generated PHP file is blocked by Drupal's stock .htaccess on a stock Apache deployment, a path-handling weakness in the Apache RewriteRule could be exploited to achieve arbitrary PHP execution. "Starting from three system-wide limits, we showed how errors that appear to affect only availability can become primitives for crossing a security boundary," Searchlight Cyber researchers Kevin Gervot and Adam Kues said. "In Drupal, temporary database failures can produce a FAIL, FAIL, and then SUCCESS sequence that reopens the installer on an existing website and ultimately leads to pre-authentication RCE through an SQLite database containing PHP code." The issue has been addressed in the following versions - - Drupal 11.4.x - Update to Drupal 11.4.13 - Drupal 11.3.x - Update to Drupal 11.3.22 - Drupal 10.6.x - Update to Drupal 10.6.22 The addition of CVE-2026-132165 to the KEV catalog follows a report received by the Drupal Security Team that it "was exploited on live sites as early as 2026-11-19 19:00 UTC." It's worth noting that CVE-2026-132165 is the third Drupal flaw to come under active exploitation this year following CVE-2026-9082 (CVSS score: 6.5) and CVE-2026-118539 (CVSS score: 6.5).

history.title: InfraTrust warns of exploited supply chain flaws in network appliances
history.text: Eclypsium's November InfraTrust report warns that most infrastructure security advisories addressing exploited vulnerabilities over the past month involve flaws in third-party software bundled into products rather than code developed by the vendors themselves. The November InfraTrust Pulse report tracks 373 new security advisories published by 23 infrastructure vendors between October 15 and November 19, covering 3,880 vulnerabilities. Of these advisories, 98 were rated critical, and 38 contained vulnerabilities listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. However, 33 of those 38 advisories fixed exploited flaws in bundled software components, primarily PHP, Node.js, and OpenSSH. These vulnerabilities pose additional risks for enterprises, as even after a software developer releases a security fix, organizations must wait for infrastructure vendors to incorporate it into their products. "Your exposure to exploited flaws depends on how quickly each vendor rebuilds its products after an upstream fix ships," the report reads. An example of this is the two PHP vulnerabilities known as PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) highlighted in last month's InfraTrust report, which are now being exploited in attacks against Palo Alto Networks and Check Point firewalls. In both cases, threat actors chained the PHP vulnerabilities with other flaws to gain root access to compromised devices, with Check Point reporting destructive attacks that deployed data-wiping malware on VMware ESXi hosts. As of November 20, PHP2Shell fixes were either partially available or had yet to be released for affected products from Fortinet, Juniper, Lenovo, HPE, Netgear, HP, and Siemens. The November 19 release of another 18 PHP security advisories further complicated patching efforts for infrastructure vendors and their customers. With administrators dealing with an increasing number of infrastructure vulnerabilities to address, InfraTrust says to prioritize the following flaws for immediate patching this month: - Cisco Expressway: CVE-2026-76466, a critical vulnerability added to CISA's KEV catalog on November 20. On November 23rd, CISA flagged this flaw as actively exploited after Russian cybersecurity firm F6 spotted hackers using it to gain root privileges. - Palo Alto Networks and Check Point: The PHP2Shell vulnerabilities and CVE-2026-123039 in Check Point gateways. Check Point warned that this flaw was being actively exploited to gain root privileges and establish persistence on vulnerable devices since late October. - Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator: CVE-2026-114625, a critical vulnerability with a CVSS score of 9.9 that was exploited in zero-day attacks. - Cisco Secure Firewall ASA and FTD: CVE-2026-76418, affecting devices configured for remote-access VPNs. The flaw was exploited in attacks to crash devices. - SonicWall SonicOS: CVE-2026-19868, allowing multifactor authentication bypass on VPNs configured with single sign-on. SonicWall warned that it received reports that the flaw was exploited in zero-day attacks. Administrators should also prioritize installing Fortinet's October hardening updates, which addressed numerous vulnerabilities discovered using AI models. As AI makes it easier to discover and exploit vulnerabilities, InfraTrust warns that organizations must take additional steps to protect their devices while waiting for vendors to release security updates. These include removing management interfaces from the Internet, segmenting them internally to limit lateral movement, and investigating previously exposed devices for backdoors that may remain even after security updates are installed. "Patching is table stakes, but what you do before the patch is available and after the exploit hits will determine whether you survive," the report concludes. Also mentions Fortinet's October hardening updates. But are these presented as fixes/workarounds for the main issue? The article mostly discusses the problem of delayed vendor incorporation of upstream fixes, and lists prioritized vulnerabilities to patch. It does state some fixes are partially available or recently released, but I need to see if there's a clear "fix or workaround" statement that I should add as a "Fix:" line.
