history.title: Hackers Compromise 24 Check Point Management Servers in Suspected AI-Driven Attack Campaign
history.text: An unknown threat actor has been using artificial intelligence (AI)-driven offensive tooling in a campaign targeting Check Point Security Management servers, impacting 22 distinct organizations across the world. The intrusion activity, tracked by GreyNoise under the moniker GreyNoise Threat 13 (GT13), is assessed to have targeted organizations in the financial services, energy, government, transportation, mining, engineering, and manufacturing sectors across the U.K., Ireland, France, Netherlands, Greece, Germany, Austria, Bulgaria, Poland, India, Thailand, Vietnam, South Korea, Hong Kong, China, Australia, and the U.S. Confirmed attack activity has been recorded between October 17 and November 2, 2026, with the threat actor using 99 IP addresses to conduct scanning, exploitation, and control. Most of these IP addresses are associated with disposable network infrastructure. The campaign has not been attributed to any known threat actor or group. It's suspected that the attackers are relying on agentic harnesses and systems for vulnerability scanning, exploitation, and automatic interaction with compromised assets. The threat actor has also been observed using tools like Nmap, Chisel, Impacket, Paramiko, and other Python scripts to carry out internal reconnaissance, privilege escalation, and lateral movement on victim environments. "We witnessed the GT13 actor use 99 IP addresses, all of which were either egresses through ExpressVPN or compromised victim Check Point devices, including activity over 1400+ network sessions, 800+ command line artifacts, and 1200+ files downloaded, uploaded, or created," GreyNoise said. In one case, the attackers have been found using an automated scanning and exploitation pipeline to compromise an HFS server using CVE-2026-61500, a critical flaw in Rejetto HFS, in early October 2026 to obtain control of the server and issue commands, including adding an SSH key to the "/root/.ssh/authorized_keys" file. Subsequently, GT13 is said to have used the compromised server as a relay for follow-on operations centered around saving command results and exfiltrating data from 24 previously compromised Check Point Security Management servers. The attackers also unsuccessfully attempted to deploy a Linux implant named ZULT to the compromised Rejetto HFS server. "The GT13 adversary had access to the victim Check Point Security Management Servers before they compromised the HFS server," the cybersecurity company said. "We could not determine when or how the attacker gained access to those Check Point assets." The attackers also moved to burrow deeper into one of the victim networks, using a script for a now-patched Check Point flaw (CVE-2026-16232) to launch over 100 management tasks on multiple Check Point Management Servers to - - Steal firewall databases and internal certificate authority files - Mint a new certificate - Unload security policies, effectively disabling firewall protections - Conduct internal network reconnaissance and attempt lateral movement The post-compromise activity also involved attempts to target other enterprise systems, such as Citrix NetScaler (CVE-2023-4966), Ivanti Connect Secure (CVE-2024-21893), VMware vCenter (CVE-2021-21972 and CVE-2023-34048), Microsoft Exchange (CVE-2021-26855 and CVE-2021-34473), and Microsoft Netlogon (CVE-2020-1472). In tandem, the threat actor has attempted to exploit various other security flaws, including, but not limited to - - CVE-2024-21893 (Ivanti Connect Secure) - CVE-2025-5777 (Citrix NetScaler) - CVE-2026-41089 (Windows Netlogon) - CVE-2026-98432 (Linux IPv4 UAF) GreyNoise has theorized that GT13 has in its possession a "mature AI-enabled offensive apparatus" that it uses to weaponize vulnerabilities, scan for susceptible assets, and exploit them to gain access to systems that can be later used as operational relays or true targets. "The activity reported by the GreyNoise article involves CVE-2026-16232, a previously disclosed vulnerability with patches already available, and does not represent a new vulnerability or exploitation technique," Sergey Shykevich, Director, Threat Intelligence at Check Point Software Technologies, told The Hacker News. "Our priority remains ensuring customers apply the available updates and follow Check Point’s published hardening guidance to restrict management access and identify suspicious activity."
history.summary: A threat actor used AI-driven tooling to compromise 24 Check Point Security Management servers across 22 organizations globally, leveraging 99 IP addresses and tools like Nmap, Chisel, and Impacket for scanning, exploitation, and lateral movement. The campaign, tracked as GT13, began in October 2026 and involved using apatched Check Point flaw (CVE-2026-16232) to steal firewall databases, mint certificates, and disable security policies on multiple management servers, while also exploiting other CVEs including CVE-2026-61500 on a Rejetto HFS server used as a relay for data exfiltration. Fix: Check Point recommends applying available updates and following published hardening guidance to restrict management access and detect suspicious activity.

history.title: Hackers Exploited CVSS 10.0 Hex.pm RCE Flaw to Compromise 6 Package Registry Servers
history.text: An attacker ran operating system commands on Monday on six production servers of Hex.pm, the package registry that Elixir and Erlang developers fetch their dependencies from. The flaw used in the attack had been in the registry's code since February 2016, and the team that maintains the service had every server on a patched build within about 15 minutes of the first malicious request. Checks since then found no sign that any package was changed. Whether the attacker read account data such as email addresses, password hashes, and two-factor authentication secrets could not be ruled out, the team said. What Hex Users Should Do Now Everyone with a hex.pm account has been logged out because the maintainers replaced the keys that sign sessions and access tokens. They advise account holders to take these steps: - Change your hex.pm password. - Reset two-factor authentication by setting up a new authenticator entry, and store the new recovery codes. - Log back in to the client with mix hex.user auth or, for Erlang projects, rebar3 hex user auth. - Update the Hex client when the next release ships, expected within days, with a new registry signing system. - Watch for phishing. Exposed email addresses may be misused, so check that links in any email about Hex go to hex.pm. API keys do not need to be replaced, according to the team: they are random 128-bit values stored only as HMAC-SHA256 hashes, which it says cannot realistically be brute-forced. Passwords are hashed with bcrypt, which slows guessing but does not stop it for weak passwords, so changing them still matters. Developers who never created a hex.pm account and only fetch public packages have nothing to reset, Peter Ullrich, one of the report's authors, said in a maintainer clarification on the Elixir Forum. Those who signed up with GitHub should still log back in to their clients, and reset two-factor authentication if they enabled it. Until the new client ships, the advice is to fetch packages only from repo.hex.pm and to avoid third-party mirrors. The registry signing key has not yet been replaced, and it was among the credentials the attacker could have read. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-129514 with the maximum CVSS score of 10.0, sat in the parser hex.pm used to read request bodies sent in an Erlang data format. That parser ran before routing and authentication, so an unauthenticated POST request to any address on the site could reach it. The decoding function was meant to be safe, and it did block dangerous terms such as functions, but it accepted maps with a __struct__ key, which allowed a request body to pose as any Elixir struct the application had loaded. The safety check that would have stopped this was removed from the code on February 23, 2016, which is where the flaw's age comes from. Exploitation before Monday has not been established. A crafted struct ran nothing by itself. It caused an error, and the error reporting code then inspected the struct. That inspection, via the Ecto and DBConnection database libraries, led to a point where the server called a function of the attacker's choice, which then ran operating system commands with the permissions of the registry's service account. The security advisory lists hex.pm as affected from February 23, 2016 until Monday. The fix commit makes the decoder reject any term containing a map with a __struct__ key, and every hex.pm server was running it by 18:31 UTC on Monday. Load balancer logs recorded 69 exploit requests between 18:16 and 18:29 UTC on Monday, all from two addresses, the Hex.pm team said in its incident report yesterday. Files created by the exploit appeared on six web servers, in one case just 3 milliseconds after the request. Three of those servers joined mid-attack, when a restart brought up machines still on the vulnerable build. To check the packages, the team compared every database table against a copy taken two minutes before the first exploit request and traced each difference to normal activity. The 23 releases published during the attack all match the audit log, no older release was changed, and the package and registry files written that evening match the database records. Database reads, shell commands, environment variables and direct reads from file storage were not logged. For that reason, "we cannot rule out that the attacker accessed data stored in the database," the team wrote. That database holds email addresses, password hashes, API key hashes, two-factor authentication secrets and session data, and private packages could also have been read without leaving a trace. The checks found no leftover shells and no new accounts or cloud keys in the audit logs. Who was behind the attack is unknown. Activity from the two addresses going back to late last week suggests the attacker built a local copy of hex.pm to test against, according to the team. A separate security report describing the same flaw arrived by email at 19:07 UTC on Monday, after the attack had ended. By yesterday morning the team had replaced every credential the attacker could have read except the registry signing key. On Monday night it reported the breach to the Swedish data protection authority, to CISA in the United States and to ENISA in the European Union. Related Library Fixes Alongside the incident, maintainers of three widely used Elixir libraries disclosed flaws of their own involving structs built from untrusted data, and shipped fixed versions yesterday. These are separate disclosures, not further attacks on Hex.pm. Each needs its own conditions to be exploited. The Ash flaw requires keyset pagination with a client-supplied cursor, certain sort field types, and a signing secret left at its unset default, according to the Ash advisory. The db_connection flaw "is not exploitable in db_connection alone," the DBConnection advisory says, because another component must first decode untrusted data into structs. The Flop flaw has similar conditions around its pagination cursors, according to the Flop advisory. The exploited flaw sits in the hexpm server code, not in the Hex client, so organizations that run their own copy of the registry are affected until they deploy the patch.
history.summary: Attackers exploited a CVSS 10.0 flaw (CVE-2026-129514) in Hex.pm's request body parser to run operating system commands on six production servers. The vulnerability, present since February 2016, allowed unauthenticated requests to manipulate Elixir structs via maps with a struct key, triggering command execution through error reporting in Ecto and DBConnection. The Hex.pm team patched all servers within 15 minutes of the attack and rejected maps containing a struct key in the decoder.

history.title: WordPress Blocks Six Backdoored WP Connect Plugins Before Malicious Releases Go Live
history.text: WordPress has removed six WordPress plugins developed by WP Connect after they were backdoored on November 22, 2026, to enable arbitrary code execution on sites that have them installed, following a suspected compromise of the developer's account. The WordPress plugins team has proactively detected and blocked the threat before it could be officially released. Visiting each plugin listing now serves the message: "This plugin has been closed as of November 22, 2026, and is not available for download. This closure is permanent." The names of the affected plugins and the malicious versions are listed below - - Air WP Sync – Airtable to WordPress (2.9.1 – 2.9.4) - WP Sync for Notion – Notion to WordPress (1.7.4) - Add-on Brevo for Gravity Forms (2.6.3) - Add-On for Contact Form 7 to Airtable (2.5.4) - Add-On for Contact Form 7 to Notion (1.6.4) - Orders Sync to Airtable for WooCommerce (1.0.2) These plugins have been collectively installed on more than 3,600 WordPress sites, according to WordPress security company Wordfence. The supply chain compromise is being tracked as CVE-2026-135202 (CVSS score: 9.8). It remains unpatched. "Each release silently loaded the same remote-control module, which phones home to an attacker-controlled server, executes any PHP code it is sent, and exposes a full command set for running shell commands, stealing password hashes, and planting webshells," security researcher Chloe Chamberland said. Specifically, the plugins come with a backdoor module ("includes/airwp-online.php") that runs on every request, sends site information (site URL, PHP, WordPress, and OS versions, and the server user) to a hard-coded command-and-control server ("tascredit-pay[.]com"), and runs PHP code returned by the server via eval(). It can also perform the following actions - - Accept queued commands that run shell commands - Read, write, and delete arbitrary files - Query arbitrary database tables - Dump the users table including login, email address, and password hashes - Drop a web shell into the uploads directory or to a path of the attacker's choosing - Register an hourly WP-Cron hook that runs attacker-supplied code As a result, an unauthenticated attacker in control of the site can execute arbitrary code on the server and take complete control, facilitating credential theft and persistence through web shells and cron hooks that outlast the plugin removal. Because the malicious versions were never released and blocked due to WordPress's new cooldown protections as part of its Protect The Shire initiative, sites running these plugins are unlikely to be affected. However, it's essential that site owners check their websites to make sure that they are not running one of the compromised versions and remove them as soon as possible. "Unlike a typical vulnerability, this was not a coding mistake, and there is no patch: the malicious code was added deliberately and committed to each plugin's WordPress.org repository," Chamberland said. "Taken together, this strongly suggests that the developer's WordPress.org account was compromised and used to push the malicious releases, rather than that the vendor shipped this code intentionally." The disclosure comes as URLscan.io revealed that an unspecified WordPress site had been infected by multiple cybercriminal campaigns, with attackers attempting to disable or remove scripts belonging to competing threat actors. The site carried "thirteen separate ClickFix injections from three distinct kits [LOM, ErrTraffic, and Macfinger], alongside seven further malicious loaders," it said. "Several of the injections attempt to remove each other's code and overlays, and one injection disables another through a JavaScript naming collision. Five of the thirteen injections resolve their next-stage infrastructure from Polygon smart contracts, a technique known as EtherHiding."
history.summary: WordPress removed six WP Connect plugins backdoored on November 22, 2026, to enable arbitrary code execution before they were officially released. The supply chain compromise is tracked as CVE-2026-135202 (CVSS 9.8), and the malicious code was deliberately added via a compromised developer account with no patch available. The plugins were blocked by WordPress’s new cooldown protections (Protect The Shire), and sites running the compromised versions are unlikely to be affected but should check and remove them.

history.title: CISA Adds 10 Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
history.text: CISA Adds 10 Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog CISA has added 10 new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. - CVE-2023-25914 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Path Traversal Vulnerability - CVE-2023-25915 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Improper Input Validation Vulnerability - CVE-2025-41450 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Improper Authentication Vulnerability - CVE-2026-103406 Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) Juniper Session Smart Conductor and Session Smart Router OS Command Injection Vulnerability - CVE-2026-133275 Mitel MiCollab Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type Vulnerability - CVE-2026-133303 Mitel MiCollab XML Injection Vulnerability - CVE-2026-133311 Mitel MiCollab Weak Authentication Vulnerability - CVE-2026-133323 Mitel MiCollab OS Command Injection Vulnerability - CVE-2026-133324 Mitel MiCollab Not Failing Securely Vulnerability - CVE-2026-133469 Vates Xen Orchestra Improper Validation of Specified Type of Input Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance. This product is provided subject to this Notification and this Privacy & Use policy.

history.title: Hackers Exploit Unpatched Flaw in Defunct Idunno AntiCsrf Library
history.text: Threat actors are exploiting an unpatched vulnerability in the open source anti-CSRF library Idunno AntiCsrf for remote code execution (RCE), security researchers warn. AntiCsrf is a legacy ASP.NET module for WebForms applications that has no active maintainer and is no longer actively supported. The most recent version, 0.9.1 Beta, was released in December 2008. Tracked as CVE-2026-131914 (CVSS score of 9.3), the exploited security defect is described as an insecure deserialization bug in the processing of HTTP POST requests to ASP.NET WebForms endpoints. “Exploitation requires only a single HTTP POST request with no prior authentication or valid CSRF token. Active exploitation in the wild has been observed,” Google Cloud’s Mandiant warned on November 18. The flaw allows an attacker to supply any non-empty value in the CSRF cookie along with a Base64-encoded gadget chain to gain RCE in the context of the IIS worker process, Mandiant notes. According to preemptive cybersecurity firm WatchTowr, the issue exists because AntiCsrf does not perform sufficient checks on data from incoming form submissions before reconstructing it into program objects. “The vulnerable check runs before the application’s own page logic, so it can affect many pages on an affected site, not just ones that use a login form. A successful attack gives the attacker control over the process that runs the website, which can lead to full compromise of the server,” WatchTowr says. On Tuesday, the US cybersecurity agency CISA added CVE-2026-131914 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list, urging federal agencies to address it within three days. As no official patch is available for the vulnerability, all organizations relying on the 18-year-old AntiCsrf to validate anti-CSRF tokens on form submissions should immediately discontinue the module and transition to an actively supported solution. “WatchTowr Intel detected exploit probes across our honeypots that used creative .NET compiled gadget payloads to confirm if a given system is vulnerable. We validated the exploit and confirmed that, if the host was vulnerable, the server would be tricked into redirecting to a unique URL that would discreetly confirm control of the web server to the attacker,” WatchTowr principal threat intelligence specialist Yordan Ganchev told SecurityWeek. “There is no patch, and likely there won’t be one. Defenders should audit ASP.NET products to identify ones packaging the Idunno.AntiCSRF library and review their audit logs for signs of exploitation. Where possible, the library should be replaced in affected applications. Where that’s not possible, apply WAF rules until alternative workarounds are identified,” Ganchev added. Related: Palo Alto Networks Patches Fragnesia Flaw Used to Root Firewalls Related: Drupal Flaw Found by Anthropic Scanner Exploited in Attacks Related: phpAfterShell Vulnerability Revives PHP2Shell’s Attack Path Related: Azure Flaw Exploited to Target Secrets at Norwegian Energy Firms

history.title: Hackers Exploit Two GeoServer Flaws as Researchers Warn of Unauthenticated RCE Chains
history.text: Threat actors are actively exploiting two newly patched security flaws in GeoServer, according to watchTowr. The vulnerabilities in question are CVE-2026-120705 and CVE-2026-129243, details of which are below - - CVE-2026-120705 (CVSS score: 8.6) - An arbitrary file read vulnerability that could enable an attacker to access local text files readable by the GeoServer process or fetch adversary-selected HTTP or HTTPS URLs by means of a single unauthenticated Web Feature Service (WFS) request. - CVE-2026-129243 (CVSS score: 8.8) - An incorrect authorization vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to invoke OWS operations that are otherwise protected by service security rules. Advisories for both the flaws were published on November 24, 2026, in the following versions - - CVE-2026-120705: org.geoserver:gs-wfs-core - 3.0.2, 2.28.6, and 2.27.7 - CVE-2026-120705: org.geotools:gt-metadata - 35.2, 34.6, and 33.7 - CVE-2026-129243: org.geoserver:gs-ows - 3.0.2, 2.28.6, and 2.27.7 "Attackers sent error-based exploit probes to validate that the server is vulnerable by creating and invoking stored queries," the preemptive exposure management firm said in an X post today. Eye Security, which discovered and reported CVE-2026-120705, said the flaw can be combined with two other vulnerabilities in the same product to create an unauthenticated remote code execution chain - - CVE-2026-129245 (CVSS score: 9.2) - A use of a hard-coded signing key ("geoserver") vulnerability in the "remember me" functionality that could be exploited to forge administrator authentication. (Fixed in org.geoserver:gs-main versions 3.0.2, 2.28.6, and 2.27.7) - CVE-2026-120704 (CVSS score: 7.2) - An improper control of the generation of code vulnerability that could allow an administrator, or anyone with access to an administrator session, to execute arbitrary code as the user running GeoServer. (Fixed in org.geoserver.security:gs-sec-jdbc versions 3.0.2, 2.28.6, and 2.27.7) In a hypothetical attack chain, a bad actor can follow the steps below - - Exploit CVE-2026-120705 to access "users.xml," a file containing GeoServer usernames and password hashes, and obtain the password representation along with the static signing key extracted from the security configuration ("security/config.xml"). - Exploit CVE-2026-129245 to forge a valid administrator authentication cookie by using the predictable signing key and the stored password representation without having to know the administrator password. - Exploit CVE-2026-120704 to abuse an administrator-controlled JDBC configuration to execute code from an uploaded native library on both Linux and Windows versions of GeoServer. According to the project maintainers, CVE-2026-129245 is also part of a five-step unauthenticated remote command execution chain that involves - - CVE-2026-129244 (CVSS score: 6.9) - WFS stored query exception discloses data directory path - CVE-2026-129243 (CVSS score: 8.8) - Service security rules bypassed with a prefixed service name such as x/WFS - CVE-2026-120705 (CVSS score: 8.6) - Unauthenticated WFS GetFeatureById XML injection - CVE-2026-129245 (CVSS score: 9.2) - Predictable "remember me" key allows administrator session forgery - CVE-2026-129242 (CVSS score: 8.6) - Deserialization in JDBC user and role services allows administrator code execution "An attacker who obtains an administrator password digest, through any file disclosure or a copy of the data directory, can log in as that administrator," GeoServer maintainers said. "Changing the key in security/config.xml does not help when the same file disclosure also reveals the key." Jonah Burgess, a Senior Security Researcher at Rapid7, who goes by the online alias CryptoCat has been acknowledged for independently discovering and reporting the five-step unauthenticated remote command execution chain on August 2, 2026. "Prefixing the Web Feature Service (WFS) name, as in x/WFS, slips past the admin-only rule for stored queries. GeoServer turns escaped text in a saved query into live xi:include elements, which leaks the files holding the remember-me key and the admin password digest," the researcher said. "Those two values forge an administrator cookie without cracking the password. As admin, the attacker points a JDBC user service at an uploaded HSQLDB database, and the bundled driver deserialises a stored value that runs commands." In light of active exploitation of two of the flaws, users are advised to update to GeoServer versions 2.27.7, 2.28.6, and 3.0.2 released over the past month as soon as possible. The development comes a little over three months after another critical flaw in GeoServer (CVE-2026-76904, CVSS score: 9.8) witnessed active exploitation efforts as a zero-day. (The story has been updated after publication to include more details of the flaws and emphasize that advisories for the issues were released on November 24, 2026. The patches were originally released in October and early November 2026.)
history.summary: Threat actors are actively exploiting two patched GeoServer vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-120705 and CVE-2026-129243, which allow arbitrary file reading and unauthorized OWS operation invocation, respectively. The flaws were disclosed on November 24, 2026, and affect specific versions of geoserver:gs-wfs-core, geotools:gt-metadata, and gs-ows. Users are advised to update to GeoServer versions 2.27.7, 2.28.6, or 3.0.2 as soon as possible. Fix: Update to GeoServer versions 2.27.7, 2.28.6, or 3.0.2.

history.title: 1Password customer data stolen after employee GitHub account breach
history.text: 1Password has disclosed a data breach after an employee's corporate GitHub account was hacked and used to deploy malicious code to the company's backend services to steal customer data. The company says customer password vaults and the encryption keys protecting them were not compromised in the attack. In a security incident disclosure published today, 1Password says it began investigating the breach on November 19 after detecting indications that an employee's GitHub account had been compromised. The attacker used the account to access private source code repositories and inject malicious code into backend services that downloaded customer account records. The stolen data includes: - Customer names and email addresses - Account and user IDs - Account creation and last sign-in timestamps - Public cryptographic keys - Secure Remote Password (SRP) protocol parameters - Invitation, provisioning, and account recovery tokens - Other internal account metadata The attacker also stole internal company source code and accessed its continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) environment, potentially exposing internal infrastructure credentials. Among the stolen customer data were tokens embedded in links that 1Password emailed to users to accept account provisioning invitations or recover their accounts. However, 1Password says these tokens cannot be used on their own to access customer accounts, as completing the invitation or recovery process requires either single sign-on (SSO) authentication or a six-digit verification code sent to the user's registered email address. The company says only a small number of users were affected and have been individually notified. As a precaution against brute-force attacks, 1Password has strengthened these verification codes from six numeric digits to ten alphanumeric characters. The company says it has now disabled the compromised GitHub account, revoked the stolen token, restored clean versions of affected services, and rotated or revoked potentially exposed infrastructure credentials. 1Password has also hired independent cybersecurity experts to validate its remediation efforts and says it has found no internal evidence of customer account takeovers. The company is not requiring customers to change their account passwords or Secret Keys but warns them to watch for unexpected invitations, account recovery requests, and other potential phishing attempts. While customer vaults were not compromised in the attack, the stolen data is valuable to threat actors as it provides a list of known 1Password users who could be targeted in phishing campaigns. Threat actors could send emails impersonating 1Password, using the breach as a lure to trick customers into disclosing their account passwords, Secret Keys, or recovery verification codes. Customers should be particularly wary of emails claiming they need to secure their accounts in response to the breach, reset their passwords, or verify their account information. Rather than clicking on links in these emails, customers should access their accounts directly through the 1Password website or app and never share their passwords, Secret Keys, or verification codes with anyone. history.title: Italy and Switzerland warn of autonomous AI-driven cyberattacks
history.text: Swiss and Italian cybersecurity agencies are warning about automated cyberattacks powered by AI agents targeting organizations in the critical infrastructure sector. The two agencies listed four AI-powered penetration testing and red-teaming frameworks that have been involved in recent breaches and hacking incidents: ARTEX AI, CyberStrikeAI, DeepSeek Harness - Red Team, and PentAGI. Both agencies have urged organizations to reduce the number of systems exposed on the internet, prioritize patching, and monitor for unusual activity. Large-scale attacks in Italy CSIRT Italia says it detected large-scale malicious campaigns that used autonomous AI agents to identify and exploit vulnerabilities and misconfigurations on exposed endpoints. In some cases, the agency observed multiple AI agents working in parallel to compromise a large number of systems within a few hours. In one instance involving a DeepSeek Harness setup, a coordinator assigned tasks to five AI agents that undertook a broad spectrum of operational stages, from information gathering to exploitation and persistence. The agents chained vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, and compromised credentials, leveraging exposed systems as a foothold to reach internal networks. “During the observed campaigns, autonomous agents demonstrated the ability to carry out complex, sustained activity to detect misconfigurations, link even low-impact vulnerabilities into complex attack chains, and dynamically adapt their operating modules,” CSIRT Italia says. “They went as far as writing malicious code in real time to evade endpoint defenses and carry out actions deeper within the infrastructure.” The Italian cybersecurity agency advises administrators to prioritize patching internet-facing systems, focus on addressing flaws known to be actively exploited in the wild, and disable remote management interfaces if not needed. The agency also recommends monitoring control plane operations, authentication sources, traffic to internal networks, and outbound server traffic to detect suspicious activity. First AI breaches in Switzerland Switzerland’s National Cyber Security Center (NCSC) warned of similar campaigns targeting organizations in the country, confirming the first cases of successful AI-assisted cyberattacks. “In recent days, the NCSC has received its first reports of cyberattacks against organisations in Switzerland in which the attack was carried out with the assistance of an AI agent,” the Swiss NCSC said. “Various organisations and operators of critical infrastructure across at least two sectors have been affected by these cyberattacks.” “In all cyberattacks known to the NCSC, the use of AI agents led to the successful compromise of the victim’s IT systems.” The agency described rapid attacks in which agents exploited weak passwords and known vulnerabilities in exposed endpoints, using frameworks to verify weaknesses and independently decide what to do next. NCSC says that the number of AI agents publicly (and often freely) available to cybercriminals has nearly doubled since October, resulting in these massive waves against Swiss organizations, including critical infrastructure operators. The agency recommends that administrators of internet-facing systems patch critical vulnerabilities within 24 hours of release, add multi-factor authentication (MFA) or passkey protection, and enforce least-privilege principles. history.title: Hackers Exploit 10 Vulnerabilities Across Mitel, Juniper, Vates, and Danfoss Products
history.text: The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Wednesday added 10 security flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, including five vulnerabilities impacting Mitel MiCollab that were disclosed last week. The Mitel MiCollab vulnerabilities are listed below - - CVE-2026-133275 (CVSS score: 5.3) - An arbitrary file upload vulnerability in the Audio, Web and Video Conferencing (AWV) Component of MiCollab that could allow an attacker to upload arbitrary files to the target system. - CVE-2026-133303 (CVSS score: 9.0) - An XML injection vulnerability in the Audio, Web and Video Conferencing (AWV) component of MiCollab that could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary commands within the context of the system. - CVE-2026-133311 (CVSS score: 5.9) - An unauthorized access vulnerability in the Audio, Web, and Video Conferencing (AWV) Component of MiCollab that could allow an attacker to obtain sensitive information. - CVE-2026-133323 (CVSS score: 10.0) - A command injection vulnerability in the Audio, Web, and Video Conferencing (AWV) Component of MiCollab that could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary commands within the context of the system. - CVE-2026-133324 (CVSS score: 5.3) - An authentication bypass vulnerability in the Audio, Web, and Video Conferencing (AWV) Component of MiCollab that could allow an attacker to bypass authentication controls and perform unauthorized actions within the context of the application. The issues affect MiCollab versions 10.3 and earlier. "Mitel provided a patch available for release 10.3 (10.3.0.18) that addresses these vulnerabilities," the company said in an advisory published November 16, 2026. "Upgrade to this release and apply the provided patch, or upgrade to a later release." Customers who are unable to apply the updates are recommended to mitigate the risk by restricting external access to the AWV component. As of writing, there are currently no details on how the vulnerabilities are being exploited in the wild. Customers who are unable to apply the updates are recommended to mitigate the risk by restricting external access to the AWV component. The addition comes against the backdrop of a report from Accenture's Apex Labs, which revealed that an unknown threat actor may have been weaponizing the flaws as zero-days as part of what's suspected to be an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted data theft campaign. Evidence indicates the deployment of a web shell against one victim organization a day before Mitel released patches, only for the intrusion to progress rapidly and allowing the threat actor to harvest credentials and steal sensitive business data from a line-of-business database server within hours. "At that victim, we found the threat actor ran its first command 12 minutes after its first request, then reached root on the MiCollab server within 30 minutes and used the directory credentials that MiCollab stores for its LDAP connector to authenticate to a domain controller within 32 minutes," Accenture said. The activity is assessed to be part of a broader campaign targeting MiCollab instances, with a second organization's MiCollab server observed holding a persistent HTTPS channel to the threat actor infrastructure since November 9, 2026. It has not been established how this server was compromised as it had been found running an older MiCollab version affected by previously disclosed flaws (i.e., MTLVULN-1694). The indicators of compromise associated with the intrusions are listed below - - 204.76.203[.]204 (Command-and-control server) - 204.76.203[.]216 - 204.76-203-204.sslip[.]io - 204.76.203[.]204/bkup/ (Data exfiltration path) - 204.76.203[.]204/bkdl/ (Tool download path) "MiCollab presents an attractive target because it is commonly internet-facing and connected to critical enterprise services, including Active Directory," Accenture said. "Its history of exploitation further underscores this risk." Also added to the KEV catalog are the following vulnerabilities - - CVE-2026-133469 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An improper validation of specified type of input vulnerability in Vates Xen Orchestra that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to bypass authentication and perform actions with administrative privileges via a specially crafted authentication token containing an empty JSON object. - CVE-2026-103406 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An operating system command injection vulnerability in Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) Juniper Session Smart Conductor and Session Smart Router that could allow a remote attacker to execute arbitrary commands as root via a specially crafted salt minion ID. The addition of CVE-2026-133469 follows an advisory from Vates VMS that the vulnerability, also tracked as VSA-2026-062, has been exploited by a threat actor from the following IP address and TOR domain - - 91.211.251[.]112:8001 - ustar3rqxgnskzgnwkgpofgtvxevm6cx3lxdbwt4mndtveqyaohid[.]onion:3333 "At least one instance of malicious exploitation of CVE-2026-103406 has been reported to the Juniper SIRT," Juniper Networks said in an advisory. "Customers are encouraged to upgrade to a fixed release as soon as possible and in the meantime take steps to mitigate this vulnerability." The remaining three security flaws relate to Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series refrigeration controllers that could lead to authentication bypass and arbitrary command execution - - CVE-2023-25914 (CVSS score: 8.8) - A path traversal vulnerability that could allow an attacker to access and read underlying server system files via the XML interface. - CVE-2023-25915 (CVSS score: 9.9) - An improper input validation vulnerability that could allow a remote attacker to run arbitrary commands on the affected system. - CVE-2025-41450 (CVSS score: 8.5) - An improper authentication vulnerability that could allow an attacker to generate a web report exposing sensitive information, including internal IP addresses, usernames, and store names. Although Danfoss makes no mention of the flaws being exploited, it's likely that they were put to use as part of high-impact attacks targeting supermarket chains across Europe in recent weeks. France has attributed the October 2026 attacks on its retail sites to Shahid Kaveh (aka Cyber Aveng3rs and Cyber Isnaad Front), an Iranian cyber unit affiliated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). In light of active exploitation, Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies are being advised to apply the necessary fixes for all the flaws, except CVE-2026-133311 and CVE-2025-41450, by November 28, 2026. The remaining two vulnerabilities must be addressed by December 9, 2026. CISA Warns of New Unpatched Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA Series Flaw The development comes as CISA has warned of an unpatched critical flaw in Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA Series (CVE-2026-129713, CVSS score: 9.8 / 9.3) controllers that could be exploited to execute arbitrary code with webserver privileges. "A stack-based buffer overflow in an unauthenticated CGI handler of the Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA Series controller allows remote attackers to send specially crafted HTTP/S POST requests, leading to memory corruption, webserver restart and hypothetically potential arbitrary code execution with webserver privileges," CISA said. "Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability." Danfoss, which has issued an alert of its own, said the security flaw impacts versions 5.4.0 and earlier. A fix for the vulnerability is expected to be addressed in an upcoming software version (5.5.x). It also said it will remove the option that allows customers to disable "Strict mode" in the product. Until the fixes are available, system administrators are advised to take the following actions - - Make sure remote access to the units is possible only through a secure VPN or in general over a protected network - Configure the units to Strict mode, which ensures higher security levels on the product - Recommend using strong passwords CISA is also recommending that organizations minimize network exposure of such devices, place control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls, and isolate them from business networks. "When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available," CISA added. "Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices."
history.summary: CISA added 10 security flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, including five Mitel MiCollab vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-133275, CVE-2026-133303, CVE-2026-133311, CVE-2026-133323, CVE-2026-133324) affecting versions 10.3 and earlier, with Mitel releasing patch 10.3.0.18 on November 16, 2026, and recommending restricting external access to the AWV component for those unable to upgrade.

history.title: Drupal Warns of New Highly Critical Site Takeover Vulnerability Under Active Exploitation
history.text: Drupal has warned of a new "highly critical" security flaw impacting Drupal core that it said has been exploited in the wild. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-136716 (CVSS score: N/A), has been described as a case of improper checking for unusual or exceptional conditions. It also relates to CVE-2026-132165 aka Fail2Install in that it addresses remaining vulnerable installation states that could still be abused to facilitate site takeover even after the fix. CVE-2026-132165 "recently fixed several vulnerabilities within the Drupal core installer," Drupal maintainers said. "However, certain sites in unusual or incomplete install states remain vulnerable to site takeover following that advisory, including production sites." "It is not apparent in the user interface if a site is in the affected vulnerable state, and sites that are already compromised may no longer be in the vulnerable state." Drupal acknowledged that the vulnerability is being exploited in the wild, but emphasized that site owners who have already secured the installer ("install.php") are not impacted. Specifically, any website that left its installer remotely accessible following the fix for CVE-2026-132165 may have been compromised. Drupal is urging site administrators to take the following actions - - Check site logs for unauthorized access, including unexpected changes to or by the user 1 account - Ensure the user 1 email address is set to under their control, and consider resetting user 1's password. The issue has been remediated in the following versions - - Drupal 11.4.x - Update to Drupal 11.4.14 - Drupal 11.3.x - Update to Drupal 11.3.23 - Drupal 10.6.x - Update to Drupal 10.6.23 - Drupal 11.0.x to 11.2.x - No fix (End-of-life) - Drupal 10.5.x and below - No fix (End-of-life) After updating to the latest supported versions, it's recommended to run "update.php" to fix existing production sites in this state and secure the Drupal installer on all new and existing sites. According to statistics shared by StepSecurity, there are about 55,800 internet-facing Drupal sites as of November 26, 2026, out of which 31,500 services are running branches that are vulnerable to CVE-2026-132165 and roughly 15,000 are on the end-of-life 8 and 9 branches.

history.title: ThreatsDay: 10M NGINX Services at Risk, 250+ Malicious Extensions, AI Server Hijacking + 17 More Stories
history.text: A website can look perfectly fine to the person running it. Log out, visit the same page, and things might look different. Something similar is happening with browser extensions, where even the way you find and install one can change what it does. Checking whether software works as expected only tells you so much. Then there’s the question of who gets to use what. Stolen logins are opening doors across connected systems, while some AI servers are sitting online for anyone to use at someone else’s expense. Even software responsible for keeping the power on has found its way into an attack. Meanwhile, authorities are taking down large scam operations, extortion gangs are making comebacks, and ransomware activity is picking up. Some of the more worrying findings this week involve things most people would have little reason to suspect. The details are worth a look. The threats change every week. Subscribe, and we’ll alert you when each new ThreatsDay Bulletin is out. - Stolen credentials expose customer data Todoist has disclosed that an attacker gained unauthorized access to its production systems and retrieved some customer information on November 23, 2026. The incident affects 6% of its users. "Between November 22 and 23, an attacker used a stolen credential associated with our version control system to modify automated workflows in three repositories and obtain additional credentials," it said. During this time, they could also read our source code. Our investigation found no changes to application code. One of the credentials they obtained allowed them to change how employees access our internal systems. The attacker used it to take over an employee’s work account and gain access to our cloud infrastructure. On November 23, the attacker downloaded a file containing account information for some early Todoist users whose passwords were stored using an older hashing method. They also made targeted queries for account tokens, searched some customer content for credentials, and accessed email information through connected Todoist for Outlook accounts." - Record cybersecurity acquisition CrowdStrike said it will acquire Zscaler in a deal worth $43.9 billion, making it the biggest cybersecurity acquisition on record. "Security used to be about keeping the adversary out. Today, safety is required to let AI in," CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz said. "The network used to connect people to places. Now it connects agents to data. With Zscaler, we're building cybersecurity's operating system: a single control plane to deploy AI, control AI, and enable any agentic application to run safely. We see a path to become the largest AI safety and security company the world has ever seen." - Paid ads activate hidden payloads Microsoft's Edge Extensions Security Team has documented SleeperWidget, a set of over 250 extensions across Microsoft Edge Add-ons, Chrome Web Store, and Mozilla Add-ons that work as advertised unless installed through a paid search ad. Once installed that way, they collect browsing data, inject ads, and change shopping links. "Its extensions pose as maps, recipe finders, package trackers, and other everyday tools. Most deliver the features they advertise, which makes hidden behavior easier to miss," it said. "In the extensions we analyzed, installation through a paid-advertising funnel also activated browsing-data collection, ad injection, and shopping-link modification." - LLMjacking without exploits An analysis of 20,354 internet-facing hosts has revealed that thousands of servers where AI services or notebook APIs have been deployed and left accessible without authentication, potentially enabling attackers to abuse them for their own purposes. "More than half of the exposed Ollama servers in this scan have already been touched by someone who is not the owner," Rapid7 said. "79% of exposed Ollama hosts list at least one :cloud model, mostly GLM, DeepSeek, MiniMax and Kimi variants. An exposed, signed-in server can provide access to someone else's paid subscription, with the bill landing on the owner. This is the self-hosted version of LLMjacking, and it requires no exploit at all." - Blockchain-backed malware delivery SonicWall Capture Labs has disclosed details of a Java-based loader from SilentNet, a Java-based remote access trojan and infostealer sold as a malware-as-a-service offering that's advertised on YouTube. The JAR masquerades as a mod for Minecraft Fabric and targets players who download mods from external sources. "Once loaded by the game, it pulls the player's Minecraft session token from memory. It then gets its command-and-control (C2) address from a smart contract on the Polygon blockchain, and downloads a portable Python runtime hidden inside a PNG image to run a second-stage infostealer," SoniWall said. "Every string in the JAR is hidden by per-character arithmetic; it resolves hostnames through DNS-over-HTTPS, and it talks to its C2 through a custom HTTPS client that skips certificate validation." - AI-powered phishing infrastructure Threat actors are using DeepSite, Hugging Face's AI website builder, to create dozens of phishing and credential-stealing pages on Hugging Face Spaces impersonating 28 brands, including Microsoft, Google, PayPal, Chase, and Coinbase. "29 of the pages were built with DeepSite, Hugging Face’s AI website builder," Aikido said. "One Microsoft login clone took about 90 minutes of plain-language prompts, and other operators asked the builder to hide their pages from crawlers or send stolen logins to Telegram." - Credential theft spans 127 CVEs According to VulnCheck, requests to steal credentials made up 13% of all vulnerability exploitation recorded between January and November 2026. Credential-harvesting attempts appeared across 127 of 694 CVEs observed in its honeypot network, with open-source software and AI developer tools like Apache, Laravel, Langflow, Flowise, MLflow, and n8n taking up 61% of the CVEs associated with credential-harvesting attempts. "Attackers search application files, logs and environment variables for database passwords, cloud credentials and API keys, with file-read and SSRF vulnerabilities providing opportunities without code execution," VulnCheck said, adding it "observed 1,756 attempts targeting AI provider and coding agent credentials from 406 IP addresses across 27 CVEs." - Ransomware disrupts critical services A previously unknown ransomware and data-extortion group calling itself BYOD has claimed at least nine organizations between October 5 and November 9, 2026. "Its attacks have had real-world consequences, including ambulance diversion, more than 30 clinics closed, and campus-wide device shutdowns," TrendAI said. "BYOD runs a pressure campaign alongside the intrusion: audio messages on infected computers, public leak-site posts, statements framing its attacks as holding organizations accountable, and outreach to individual victims." Although the complete intrusion chain remains to be analyzed, evidence points to credential compromise and a remote access trojan on an employee's computer for initial access. - Malicious JavaScript delivery platform A malware campaign has been observed installing a fake WordPress plugin built almost entirely by a name generator, including its title, directories, files, and functions (e.g., trijavascriptly, ultravueal, maxdataic, and quadmicroservicesion). "Behind the generated names is a second-stage delivery platform that runs arbitrary JavaScript in the browser of every anonymous visitor to an infected site, routes that traffic through the victim's own domain, and lies dormant for logged-in users," Wordfence said. The malware has been discovered twice, once in January 2026 and another in September 2026. Exactly how the plugin is installed is not known, but investigation shows that it's likely via a compromise of an administrator account. - Global scam networks disrupted The U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) has announced that over 17.3 million scam accounts have been deplatformed on Meta, 700 fraudulent crypto investment websites seized, and 12 U.S. arrest warrants issued as part of efforts to tackle foreign and domestic scams over the past six months. The Strike Force has traced and restrained $1,082,260,156.82 in cryptocurrency stolen from U.S. victims. "Our Scam Center Strike Force has continued its work investigating cyber-enabled fraud perpetrated against Americans by transnational organized crime groups, emanating out of Asia and attacking America's main street," said U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro. "The Strike Force teams focus on identifying and pursuing key leaders — including Chinese organized crime affiliates operating in Cambodia, Laos, and Burma, and rapidly expanding around the globe — to bring them to justice." FBI Director Kash Patel said the Operation Blackout scam demolition initiative has "seized nearly $17 billion in illicit funds, taken more than 14,000 digital devices, directly warned over 11,000 Americans from scam attempts, and prevented more than $690 million in potential victim losses." Over 29 scam compounds operating across Asia, Africa, and the Middle East have been dismantled and more than 2,200 trafficked workers have been repatriated. The U.S. State Department has also worked with U.S. and Southeast Asian law enforcement to facilitate the freezing of more than $1 billion in stolen cryptocurrency, the takedown of over 1.4 million fraudulent websites and accounts, and several arrests. Earlier this month, the U.S. Attorney's Office also filed a civil forfeiture action to recover 456,602 USDT (Tether) that's alleged to be proceeds of romance fraud schemes targeting individuals in Massachusetts and elsewhere on online dating sites and Facebook. - Billion-dollar crypto recovery bid The Justice Department has filed a civil action to recover over $1.1 billion in cryptocurrency that was illicitly obtained from Binance by North Korean actors in a major hack last month. history.title: FIFA Says It Has Been Victim of a Cyberattack Accessing ‘Personal and Business Information’
history.text: FIFA was the victim of a cyberattack that saw hackers gain access to what soccer’s world governing body describes as a “limited set of personal and business information,” it said Thursday. “FIFA is working closely with the relevant authorities, including law enforcement,” the organization said in a statement sent to The Associated Press. FIFA didn’t say when the cyberattack took place, or the precise nature of the hacked information. Last week, a group calling itself the Handsome Boy Hacking Club posted a screenshot on X of what it claimed were FIFA files. Three days later, it appeared to take credit for the hack when responding to a post that said more than 12 gigabytes of internal documents had been leaked. “FIFA condemns in the strongest possible terms the unlawful acquisition and publication of information, particularly personal data,” the governing body said in its statement. “Such actions constitute a serious and unacceptable violation of privacy and can have significant consequences for the individuals concerned.” The breach comes at a time when FIFA and its president, Gianni Infantino, is under scrutiny after his foiled, secretive plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors. Infantino is also trying to extend his 11-year presidency of FIFA to 2031. He is the favorite when the election is held on March 18, with Kohzo Tashima of Japan and Philippe Diallo of France the other candidates. Related: 1Password Breach Exposes Customer Data, Internal Source Code Related: US Treasury’s FinCEN Disconnects Systems Following Cyber Incident Related: Plagiarism Checker Turnitin Investigating Cyberattack
history.summary: FIFA confirmed it was victim of a cyberattack that gave hackers access to a limited set of personal and business information. The organization stated it is working closely with relevant authorities and law enforcement to address the breach. A group calling itself the Handsome Boy Hacking Club claimed responsibility for the attack.

history.title: North Korea-Linked PolinRider Poisons Over 7,600 GitHub Repositories to Spread Malware
history.text: The threat actors behind the PolinRider campaign have been observed planting a Python loader in GitHub repositories, as evidence emerges that the activity may have started as far back as February 2025. "The loader hides in a small utils package or in conftest.py," SafeDep said in a report published this week. "When Python imports the file, the loader reads the newest transaction that an Ethereum wallet sent to itself. It decodes the input data of that transaction as JavaScript and runs it with Node.js." The JavaScript code, for its part, reads a second wallet to locate the command-and-control (C2) server and then passes the next stage to a detached interactive Node.js environment by means of a node -i process. The software supply chain security company said it identified the loader in 375 public repositories that belong to 260 accounts. There is no evidence that the loader has been distributed via PyPI or npm. PolinRider is the name assigned to a malicious campaign linked to North Korean threat actors. Recent reports indicate that the activity employs various channels to distribute malware, including - - Fraudulent recruitment campaigns that make use of phishing emails and fake hiring portals like BlockNovas, AccuraSoftHire ("accurasofthire[.]com") and HuntRole ("huntrole[.]org") to trick prospective targets into running malware-laced projects under the pretext of a take-home assessment. - Publishing malicious packages across open-source ecosystems by hijacking maintainer accounts to plant obfuscated malware through fake font files (fa-solid-400.woff2, fa-solid-500.woff2, or fa-solid-300.llf), Visual Studio Code (VS Code) auto-run tasks, and Git history rewriting. - Using compromised developer machines to steal their GitHub tokens and force-push malicious commits into open-source repositories they have access to. At a high level, the PolinRider loader retrieves an encrypted second-stage Node.js payload that scans the infected host for installed developer applications, such as GitHub Desktop, Cursor, VS Code, and Google Antigravity, and tampers with the most frequently used tools to execute attacker-controlled code and deliver infostealer malware. It's worth noting here that PolinRider is assessed to be a sub-cluster operating in parallel with a long-running campaign codenamed Contagious Interview. While the latter is more of a social-engineering entry point that's used to compromise developer systems, PolinRider abuses the access to modify repositories and turn them into a distribution channel for malware. "Cybercriminal groups deploy supply chain worms for opportunistic theft. On the other hand, North Korean state-sponsored threat actors use open-source software registries as a primary initial access vector targeting corporate environments," Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 said in a report published last month. "Threat actors demonstrate how compromising a single maintainer account or registry scope converts open-source dependencies, resulting in widespread affected cloud environments." Some of the decoy sites have been found to incorporate two other alternate delivery paths - - Instruct candidates to sideload a Google Chrome extension after enabling "Developer mode" to subscribe to new job alerts. - Employ ClickFix-style lures to get victims to copy and paste malicious commands into the terminal app depending on the operating system as part of a "standard settings bundle for candidates and interview workflows." "The [job] application asks for a short verification video," StepSecurity said. "Until the server marks a candidate as having installed a 'driver,' the camera check always fails with a message saying the system does not have a compatible camera environment." "A separate 'Technical onboarding' page on the site gives a one-line curl command to download the 'driver.' On Windows, the downloaded installer fetches a script from the careers site that installs Node.js if it is missing, downloads a JavaScript payload, runs it in the background and deletes itself. The macOS and Linux versions do the same." The JavaScript malware is designed to perform the following steps - - Read the latest transaction associated with an Ethereum wallet ("0xa322E5f3D311D3080e6f0121063e9aDC2490Ef1a"). - Get its destination wallet address ("0x67B38e9b67B38E9b68656c6C6f6970626f742121"). - Extract the C2 server address twice ("103.179.142[.]155") from the first eight bytes ("67B38e9b" and "67B38E9b") of the wallet address, using a technique referred to as NullReceiver, while the last 12 bytes represent the ASCII string "helloipbot!!." - Use the IP address to fetch two payloads, "0x/cls" and "0x/ls," over port 443. The latest findings from SafeDep show that the repositories are injected with a 58-line Python loader that reads the "0x3b1574417524c11a7403c4b232CAcBb320CceBC6" wallet to extract JavaScript code that then reaches out to a second wallet ("0x1eEf0849EDa15d87f64e51C73C8442Cf3c8bCEF3") to obtain the destination wallet associated with the latest transaction ("0x5F87b5545F87b55468656C6C6f6970626f742121"), which is then used to parse the C2 server ("95.135.181[.]84"). A defining aspect of NullReceiver is the marker "68656c6C6f6970626f742121" in the made-up destination wallet address that consistently translates to "helloipbot!!." "The /0x/cls script runs twice, once with eval in the current process and once in a new process," SafeDep said. "The /0x/ls script runs only in a new process." The exact nature of these payloads remains unknown. However, prior waves have been observed installing a stealer that harvests environment secrets, browser passwords, cookies, and wallet data. Interestingly, the wallet address "0x1eef0849eda15d87f64e51c73c8442cf3c8bcef3" has been reused by the threat actors across other attack waves - - Pushing compromised versions of legitimate npm packages such as @adminide-stack/utils, @adminide-stack/health-api-server, @adminide-stack/user-activity-browser, @adminide-stack/utils, @adminide-stack/forms-core, @adminide-stack/yantra-help-browser, server-hemera-mongo, cdeops, @cdmbase/wiki-browser, and @pubngo-stack/help-browser that use the same wallet address to fetch /0x/cls and /0x/ls from "95.135.181[.]151." - A fake recruitment campaign from HuntRole that convinces victims to complete a coding assessment, which uses a VS Code extension named "huntrole.assessment-tool" from the Visual Studio Marketplace to send system information and fetch and run a malicious JavaScript payload. The script queries the same wallet address to fetch /0x/cls and /0x/ls from "95.135.181[.]84." - Using a GitHub account named " Eternity0207 " to open over 200 pull requests targeting open-source projects like AsyncAPI Generator, CircuitVerse, and Open Food Facts, and subsequently force-push a modified commit containing an obfuscated loader that uses the same wallet address to fetch /0x/cls and /0x/ls from "95.135.181[.]84." - According to the maintainer of AsyncAPI Generator, "Each time, the payload stayed on the branch for 30-40 minutes and was then force-pushed away, so the final diff looked clean." The unauthorized modifications allowed the loader to run when an unsuspecting developer runs "npm run build" (for AsyncAPI), loads the test configuration (for Open Food Facts), or opens the folder in VS Code (for CircuitVerse). The GitHub account has since been suspended. According to estimates from Apiiro, PolinRider has been detected in at least 7,609 GitHub repos owned by 2,330 accounts, most of them belonging to developers. Some of the victims include Neutralinojs, InstaWP Connect, and fxhash. The loader has been pushed to 2,040 repositories between October 27 and November 6, 2026. "The worm uses stolen GitHub access to rewrite commits the developer already made, keeping the author, message and date, and adds a loader hidden after hundreds of spaces in a build config," Apiiro researcher Shmulik Cohen said. "Building the project runs it. In the newest wave, opening the folder in VS Code is enough. The loader reads its server from an Ethereum wallet, so taking a server down changes nothing: one transaction moves every loader to the next." The development comes as OpenSourceMalware said it discovered a PolinRider attack from May 2025, predating the earliest documented victims by eight months. The attack targeted nine packages, using hijacked maintainer account to push poisoned versions within a span of 90 minutes - - itsa-utils@1.4.2 - itsa-jsext@2.0.3 - itsa-react-docviewer@16.1.2 - itsa-cli@16.5.3 - itsa-react-button@16.0.11 - itsa-react-maskedinput@16.1.2 - itsa-react-checkbox@16.0.5 - itsa-react-focuscontainer@16.0.10 - itsa-react-input@16.1.2 Each of these packages have been found to leverage EtherHiding, a precursor to NullReceiver, to retrieve a JavaScript downloader called JADESNOW, which is then used to deliver InvisibleFerret, a Python-based backdoor used in Contagious Interview campaigns, along with a Socket.IO RAT and a Python-based stealer. "The 2025 sample carries PolinRider's payload but not its documented spread behavior, which appears in the same maintainer's GitHub repositories in four windows between January and July 2026," security researchers Paul McCarty and Jenn Gile said. "The blockchain records behind it date attacker activity back to February 2025." "The infection likely persisted on the maintainer's machine from 2025, because the 2026 pushes ran from it. That matches PolinRider's documented propagation script, which rolls back the clock, folds the payload into the tip commit, and force-pushes with the developer's own credentials."
history.summary: North Korea-linked PolinRider campaign has been planting a Python loader in over 7,600 GitHub repositories, where it hides in utility packages or conftest.py and executes malicious JavaScript by reading Ethereum wallet transaction data to locate command-and-control servers. The loader spreads through compromised developer accounts, force-pushed commits, fraudulent recruitment campaigns, and hijacked open-source packages, then tamper with frequently used developer tools like VS Code and GitHub Desktop to deliver infostealer malware. "The worm uses stolen GitHub access to rewrite commits... and opening the folder in VS Code is enough" to trigger the loader, which reads its server from an Ethereum wallet, making server takedowns ineffective.

history.title: 1Password Hacked, Customer Data and Source Code Stolen in GitHub Account Breach
history.text: Popular password management software 1Password on Wednesday disclosed a security incident involving its backend systems that led to the unauthorized access of some customer information, but emphasized that customer password vaults and other secrets were not accessed. "While we took immediate steps to contain the incident, the attacker gained access to some of our backend systems and accessed a limited amount of customer account information from a subset of our customers, including names and email addresses," the Toronto-based company said. It noted that no customer vault content, including secrets, passwords, and other vault items, account recovery keys, or the keys that secure them, was accessed or compromised as a result of the breach. It also stated that customers do not need to take any action, but cautioned them to stay vigilant against unexpected phishing attempts. As part of its efforts to remediate the incident, 1Password has disabled the affected GitHub account, revoked the stolen token, hardened GitHub, CI/CD, and endpoint controls, restored clean versions of the affected service, and rotated internal credentials. It has also lengthened the codes used in invitation and recovery emails from six digits to ten characters as a precautionary measure. According to the company, the incident dates back to November 19, 2026, when it began investigating suspicious activity after an unknown threat actor gained access to an employee's corporate GitHub account. The attacker is said to have weaponized the account to access source code and push malicious code to its backend services, resulting in the download of administrative data related to its customers, including - - Names - Email addresses - Account and user identifiers, such as account creation and last sign-in times - Public keys - Secure Remote Password protocol parameters - Tokens present in certain emailed links for invitations, provisioning, and account recovery - Non-secret internal metadata about the account, such as version numeric identifiers, file numeric identifiers 1Password also noted that the tokens embedded in the links cannot be used on their own to gain access to customer accounts, as doing so requires either single sign-on (SSO) authentication or a six-digit verification code sent to the user's registered email address. However, it noted that a small number of users were affected and have been individually notified. "The attacker also copied source code from private repositories and gained access to our CI/CD system," 1Password said. "Our source code is not customer data, and contains no user secrets. There is no impact to 1Password’s services, availability, or product security." "Your vault secrets are encrypted with keys that only you hold, so we can’t access them, and neither can an attacker who gets into our servers."
history.summary: 1Password disclosed a security incident where an attacker gained access to a corporate GitHub account, leading to unauthorized access of customer account information (names, email addresses) and source code from private repositories, but confirmed that customer vault secrets, passwords, and encryption keys were not accessed or compromised. The company stated there is no impact to service availability, product security, or user vault data, and affected users have been individually notified. 1Password remediated the incident by disabling the affected GitHub account, revoking the stolen token, hardening CI/CD and endpoint controls, restoring clean service versions, rotating internal credentials, and extending invitation and recovery email codes from six to ten characters as a precautionary measure.

history.title: 1Password Breach Exposes Customer Data, Internal Source Code
history.text: Password management and identity security company 1Password revealed on Wednesday that a hacker stole customer information and proprietary source code. 1Password says customer vaults are not affected. The company launched an investigation on November 19 after discovering that an employee’s corporate GitHub account may have been compromised. The attacker used the account to deploy malicious code to backend services and exfiltrate customer records. The compromised customer records include names, email addresses, account identifiers, public cryptographic keys, authentication parameters, account activity times, and non-secret metadata. In addition, the threat actor obtained source code from private repositories and accessed the company’s CI/CD system, potentially exposing infrastructure credentials. According to 1Password, the hacker also obtained tokens from emails sent to users for account invitations, provisioning, and recovery. A “small number” of individuals who were undergoing provisioning or recovery during the intrusion have been notified. However, the company noted that the exposed tokens cannot be exploited on their own and there is no evidence that the attacker hijacked user accounts. A 1Password representative noted on the company’s community forum that the stolen authentication data included Secure Remote Password verifiers derived from user account passwords and Secret Keys. The verifiers cannot be used directly for authentication, and brute-forcing account passwords would require the associated Secret Keys, which 1Password does not store. 1Password highlighted that customer vaults and the cryptographic keys protecting them were not compromised. “We have no evidence that encrypted vaults were downloaded or accessed,” a 1Password community manager said. The breach also does not impact client applications, browser extensions, and account recovery keys. It’s unclear how many users are affected and how the hacker gained initial access to the corporate GitHub account. In response to the intrusion, 1Password disabled the compromised GitHub account, invalidated a stolen token, replaced potentially compromised infrastructure credentials, and restored clean versions of affected services. The company said its investigation, conducted with independent cybersecurity experts, is still ongoing. Customers do not need to take any action, but have been advised to watch for phishing attacks that could exploit news of the incident. history.summary: 1Password revealed a breach where a hacker stole customer information and proprietary source code by compromising an employee's corporate GitHub account, deploying malicious code to backend services and exfiltrating records containing names, emails, account identifiers, and authentication parameters. The attacker accessed the company's CI/CD system and obtained tokens and Secure Remote Password verifiers, but 1Password confirmed that customer vaults, encryption keys, and cryptographic protections were not compromised. Fix: 1Password disabled the compromised GitHub account, invalidated the stolen token, replaced potentially compromised infrastructure credentials, and restored clean versions of affected services.

history.title: OpenAI warns GPT-6.2 Astra will hit usage limits 40% faster because it fixed a bug
history.text: OpenAI confirmed that it fixed a 'bug' that incorrectly discounted GPT-6.2 usage, which means you'll now hit GPT usage limits 40% faster than before. In a post on X, Tibo Sottiaux, who works on Codex and ChatGPT at OpenAI, admitted to a billing mistake that incorrectly discounted GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol usage for most users. OpenAI says it has fixed the issue but warned that the same tasks will now consume more of users' allowances. "We've fixed this now, so the same work will use more of your plan's usage allowance," Sottiaux explained. "Comparing to last week, you will reach your limits 40% faster on GPT-6.2 Astra and 25% faster on Sol." However, OpenAI says both models will still offer better usage efficiency than their predecessors, GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol. OpenAI is giving subscribers an extra usage reset OpenAI says it won't charge users for the usage difference caused by the mistake, but it is offering something in return for the disruption. "As a small token to apologize for the mistake, we'll be adding one banked reset for everyone on Go, Plus, Pro, and Business," Sottiaux said. I can confirm that a new reset has been added to ChatGPT, and it expires a month later. So, if you go to ChatGPT Settings > Usage and click Reset, you can restore your exhausted usage limits. As much as I appreciate OpenAI giving its users a free usage reset, it's important to understand that this isn't equivalent to getting 40% less usage. You're still going to use your tokens much faster, and it's unclear when OpenAI will reduce the costs.
